articles.title: Por que uma nova onda de soldados norte-coreanos pode lutar na Ucrânia | G1
articles.standfirst: A Coreia do Norte continuará a enviar seus soldados para lutar na guerra da Rússia contra a Ucrânia, mas apenas enquanto a colaboração trouxer benefícios para o país.
articles.summary: A Coreia do Norte continuará a enviar seus soldados para lutar na guerra da Rússia contra a Ucrânia, mas apenas enquanto a colaboração trouxer benefícios para o país.
articles.body:
Um inimigo que invadiu o campo de batalha em grandes grupos e, sob ataque, parece alheio aos perigos dos drones e disparos de armas automáticas.

Um corpo de elite de soldados fantasmas que preferem o suicídio à rendição. Eles lutam e morrem aos milhares, aparentemente desaparecendo do front.

A Coreia do Norte enviou soldados próprios para lutar ao lado das forças da Rússia , buscando repelir uma ofensiva ucraniana em território russo no final de 2024. Eles pagaram um alto preço, com até 3 mil mortos em ação, dentre os 13 mil soldados destacados para o combate.

Eles acabaram adaptando suas táticas e, ao lado da Rússia, retiraram as forças ucranianas da região russa de Kursk.

Em termos de combate, pouco se ouviu falar deles desde então. Mas, segundo o presidente ucraniano, Volodymyr Zelensky, forças norte-coreanas e suas armas devem fazer em breve um dramático retorno à guerra da Rússia contra a Ucrânia .

Em agosto, Zelensky alertou que até 50 mil militares norte-coreanos serão destacados para a Rússia, revisando uma estimativa anterior de 30 mil soldados. Ele convocou a Coreia do Sul a fornecer apoio à defesa aérea do seu país.

Mas por que, depois de tantas baixas, a Coreia do Norte enviaria mais soldados para lutar pela Rússia? E o que aconteceu com seus soldados destacados inicialmente?

"Eles ainda estão lá", segundo o pesquisador Yang Uk, do Centro de Política Externa e Segurança Nacional do Instituto Asan em Seul, na Coreia do Sul.

"Eles estão defendendo o território russo contra um novo contra-ataque da Ucrânia. E acreditamos que parte das equipes de engenheiros ou trabalhadores possa estar na região de Donbas [ocupada pela Rússia], mas não as tropas de combate."

A Diretoria Central de Inteligência do Ministério da Defesa da Ucrânia (HUR, na sigla em ucraniano) calcula que 8,5 mil militares norte-coreanos ainda estejam em território russo.

Eles são organizados em quatro brigadas, que operam como parte do Grupo de Forças "Norte". Sua missão é proteger a fronteira da Federação Russa na região de Kursk contra as incursões da Ucrânia.

"Eles não participam de operações ativas de combate", explicou a HUR, em declaração à BBC. "Não foram observadas unidades do Exército Popular Coreano em territórios ucranianos temporariamente ocupados."

Acontecimento inédito para a Coreia do Norte

Comemoração do 85º aniversário do Exército da Coreia do Norte — Foto: Kyodo/via REUTERS

Para o líder da Coreia do Norte, Kim Jong-un, o destacamento em Kursk foi uma aposta — a maior força de combate norte-coreana já enviada para o exterior na história do país.

Em 1973, a Coreia do Norte destacou 1,5 mil militares e instrutores para o Egito, durante a guerra do Yom Kippur contra Israel. E, nos anos 1960, calcula-se que 87 pilotos norte-coreanos tenham lutado pelo Vietnã do Norte contra as forças dos Estados Unidos.

Apesar do banho de sangue, a aposta foi vencedora.

O combate rendeu incontáveis benefícios para o país, isolado e empobrecido, transformando sua economia e seu exército. E poderá servir de modelo para cooperações militares ainda mais profundas.

Os norte-coreanos "agora sabem o que é o combate moderno", segundo Yang.

Extremamente isolada, a Coreia do Norte é um Estado totalitário, militarizado e fortemente doutrinado.

Inicialmente, nem a Rússia, nem a Coreia do Norte, reconheceram sua presença na guerra. As forças ucranianas lutaram contra eles pela primeira vez em novembro de 2024 e os primeiros prisioneiros de guerra norte-coreanos vivos foram capturados apenas em janeiro de 2025.

A Rússia só reconheceu a participação da Coreia do Norte na guerra na Ucrânia em abril do ano passado, quando o chefe do Estado-Maior das Forças Armadas russas, Valery Gerasimov, descreveu seu "heroísmo" no campo de batalha.

Os militares destacados para lutar na Rússia são do Storm Corps, a tropa de elite das forças armadas norte-coreanas.

"Os soldados norte-coreanos são muito corajosos, especialmente os do Storm Corps", prossegue Yang. "Eles estão dispostos a morrer pelo seu país."

"Mas o problema é que a paixão não significa técnicas de combate eficientes... [Eles sofreram] um grande banho de sangue na primeira fase da campanha de Kursk, mas aprenderam as lições da guerra moderna com drones."

"Bucha de canhão": é assim que o soldado "Sultão", da 95ª Brigada de Ataque Aéreo da Ucrânia, descreveu as tropas norte-coreanas. Ele as enfrentou na batalha de Kursk, no final de 2024.

"Eles começavam com um grande grupo de ataque, depois mais 15 a 20 homens eram enviados para a mesma posição e mais depois daqueles", descreveu ele, na capital ucraniana, Kiev.

"Os norte-coreanos operavam de forma diferente. Eles ficavam se movimentando o tempo todo. Aquilo oferecia a eles uma certa vantagem, mas que não era decisiva."

Soldados detêm armas sentados em um veículo carregando foguetes enquanto passam pelo estande com o líder norte-coreano Kim Jong Un durante desfile militar marcando o 105º aniversário de nascimento do pai fundador do país, Kim Il Sung — Foto: Reuters/Damir Sagolj

A comunicação entre eles e seus aliados russos parecia ser fraca, segundo ele. E i equipamento dos seus soldados era inadequado.

Após o combate, Sultão e seus homens revistavam os corpos inimigos em busca de documentos e informações de inteligência. Entre os mortos russos, eles encontravam pertences pessoais, identificações e equipamentos.

"Mas, quando revistávamos especificamente os norte-coreanos, tudo o que encontrávamos era munição. Verificamos absolutamente todos os bolsos pequenos e não havia documentos, nada", ele conta.

Outros soldados ucranianos relataram que os norte-coreanos não tinham coletes de proteção, nem roupas de inverno, nem capacetes.

Em um vídeo assustador de um ataque ucraniano, um soldado norte-coreano ferido aparece de bruços sobre o solo coberto de neve em um bosque.

À medida que os ucranianos se aproximam, ele detona uma granada sob seu queixo. Em suas últimas palavras, ele clamou o nome do seu líder, Kim Jong-un.

Em abril de 2025, durante uma cerimônia memorial no recém-criado Museu de Operações Militares Estrangeiras, Kim elogiou os heróis que optaram pelo suicídio, em vez da captura.

Em discurso aos parentes dos soldados, ao lado do ministro da Defesa da Rússia, Andrey Belousov, ele os descreveu como "heróis que preferiram, sem hesitar, a autodetonação e ataques suicidas, para defender a honra maior".

O museu fica na capital norte-coreana, Pyongyang.

A Coreia do Norte nunca reconheceu oficialmente a contagem de mortos da operação em Kursk. Mas uma análise do memorial feita pela BBC News Coreia calculou que 2,3 mil soldados norte-coreanos tenham sido mortos lutando pela Rússia.

O braço de inteligência da Ucrânia, HUR, estima em 3 mil mortos e 1,5 mil feridos.

Mas, além da experiência de combate, por que a Coreia do Norte sacrificou tantos dos seus melhores soldados em uma guerra no exterior?

O líder norte-coreano, Kim Jong-Un, aperta a mão do presidente russo, Vladimir Putin, durante uma cerimônia para marcar o 80º aniversário do fim da Segunda Guerra Mundial, em 2025 — Foto: KCNA via Reuters

O deslocamento do exército norte-coreano trouxe vantagens econômicas que eram muito necessárias para o país, além de uma vitória geopolítica, segundo o pesquisador sênior Lim Soo-ho, do Instituto de Estratégias de Segurança Nacional em Seul, na Coreia do Sul.

Ele calcula que as vendas de armas para a Rússia e o destacamento de tropas tenham gerado para o país empobrecido cerca de US$ 10 bilhões (cerca de R$ 51,5 bilhões).

"O PIB anual da Coreia do Norte é calculado em cerca de US$ 30 bilhões", cerca de R$ 155 bilhões, segundo Lim.

"Isso significa que eles ganharam um terço do PIB anual em dois anos e meio de exportações de armas e destacamento de tropas, o que, para uma economia pequena como a da Coreia do Norte, é muito significativo."

Em troca dos soldados, a Coreia do Norte recebe alimentos, petróleo e moeda estrangeira.

A China afirma que respeita as sanções impostas a Pyongyang, ao contrário da Rússia. E a cooperação com Moscou fez com que Pyongyang reduzisse sua longa dependência de Pequim, o que é igualmente importante.

Em setembro do ano passado, Kim Jong-un conseguiu ficar lado a lado em Pequim com o líder chinês Xi Jinping e o presidente da Rússia, Vladimir Putin. Foi a primeira reunião pública dos três líderes.

Kim não era exatamente um igual, mas não dependia mais exclusivamente da China.

Este fato é significativo, segundo Lim. "É uma importante mudança geopolítica."

"Sempre que tudo ficava difícil devido ao isolamento, a Coreia do Norte se voltava, em primeiro lugar, à Coreia do Sul, ao Japão ou, especialmente, aos Estados Unidos, para tentar normalizar as relações. Este era o padrão da diplomacia na península coreana.

"Mas, agora, com os laços mais próximos com a Rússia, Kim Jong-un defende que o mundo vive uma nova Guerra Fria, um sistema multipolar", explica o pesquisador.

O acordo com a Rússia começou como uma oportunidade econômica e militar. Agora, ele parece estar se desenvolvendo para se tornar algo mais profundo e duradouro.

Durante o nono Congresso do Partido dos Trabalhadores da Coreia do Norte, neste ano, Kim Jong-un falou entusiasticamente sobre feitos nunca antes realizados pelo seu avô, Kim Il-sung (1912-1994), nem pelo seu pai, Kim Jong-il (1941-2011).

O líder norte-coreano, Kim Jong-un, durante exercício militar da Coreia do Norte, em imagem de arquivo. — Foto: Reprodução/ Reuters

Até agora, nenhum soldado norte-coreano lutou em território ucraniano, mesmo nas regiões ocupadas pela Rússia. Se isso acontecesse, haveria consequências diplomáticas pelo menos na Coreia do Sul, aliada da Ucrânia, que forneceu apenas assistência "não letal" até agora.

O presidente Zelensky destacou este ponto ao pressionar Seul em busca de equipamento militar avançado, incluindo sistemas de defesa aérea.

Ele declarou que, desde junho, existem preparativos em andamento na região russa de Voronezh para receber novos soldados norte-coreanos. Zelensky afirma que Pyongyang estaria se preparando para transferir novas armas balísticas para a Rússia.

"A Rússia está ajudando a Coreia do Norte a aprender sobre equipamentos bélicos modernos, melhorar suas armas e ganhar experiência real em combate", declarou ele, em julho. "Isso representa uma ameaça para todos os países da Ásia que se encontram dentro do alcance dos mísseis norte-coreanos."

Apenas dois soldados da Coreia do Norte foram capturados vivos em batalhas contra forças ucranianas. É um número surpreendentemente baixo, já que 11 mil a 14 mil militares do país combateram na campanha de Kursk.

Um terceiro soldado norte-coreano foi capturado vivo, mas morreu devido a lesões relativas aos combates, segundo o Serviço Nacional de Inteligência da Coreia do Sul.

Como seus colegas que preferiram o suicídio à captura, nenhum dos homens pretendia ser levado vivo.

"Para os soldados de Joseon [Coreia do Norte], ser prisioneiro de guerra, por si só, é crime. Simplesmente não é uma opção. Não podemos ser prisioneiros de guerra", declarou um dos homens capturados à equipe de produção de um documentário da rede pública sul-coreana MBC, em entrevista na prisão ucraniana.

Baek Pyeong-gang (nome fictício) foi atingido por um ataque de drone e permaneceu quatro dias ferido até ser capturado. Ele foi levado a se render ao confundir soldados ucranianos com seus aliados russos.

O segundo prisioneiro, Lee Kang-eun (outro nome fictício), declarou à jornalista Kim Young-mi que se sentia culpado por ainda estar vivo. Ele mal estava consciente quando soldados ucranianos o encontraram no campo de batalha, com extensas lesões em um dos braços e na mandíbula.

"Eu não tinha granada nem facas para pôr fim à minha vida", contou ele.

Lee descreveu que muitos dos seus colegas foram mortos por drones no início da guerra. O campo de batalha "cheirava a sangue", segundo ele.

Nenhum dos homens deseja retornar à Coreia do Norte. Lee afirmou acreditar que seus familiares seriam "eliminados", como punição pela sua captura.

Ambos declararam que querem ser enviados para a Coreia do Sul, que está disposta a recebê-los.

Apenas a Rússia pediu o retorno dos soldados, não Pyongyang.

Mas a Ucrânia ainda tenta pressionar Seul em busca de auxílio militar. Por isso, o país não se comprometeu a entregá-los às autoridades sul-coreanas.

Kiev declarou que irá cumprir com suas obrigações com base nos direitos humanos internacionais, que impedem a repatriação forçada de prisioneiros de guerra.

O destino dos dois soldados ainda não foi decidido. Mas o que parece certo é que outros norte-coreanos ainda irão participar da guerra, ao lado da Rússia.

A importância política e econômica dos seus serviços para Pyongyang é imensa, mas Moscou também precisa deles desesperadamente. Quatro anos e meio depois da invasão da Ucrânia, a Rússia enfrenta imensa falta de combatentes.

Agências de inteligência ucranianas e ocidentais calculam que Moscou venha perdendo mensalmente cerca de 6 mil soldados a mais do que consegue recrutar. E, para preservar seu contingente, a Rússia foi forçada a recorrer a combatentes estrangeiros, vindos da Colômbia, Quênia, Camarões e Coreia do Norte.

Para Moscou e Pyongyang, o relacionamento é mutuamente benéfico: uma coalizão que tem um preço.

Por isso, a Coreia do Norte continuará enviando seus soldados para lutar na guerra da Rússia, mas só enquanto a colaboração for lucrativa.

articles.title: Quem era o pai que morreu no lago depois de cair junto com o filho | G1
articles.standfirst: Fagner Lima liderava uma igreja evangélica de Buriti Alegre e era conhecido pela sua dedicação à esposa e ao único filho. Bombeiros ainda buscam o corpo do menino de 4 anos.
articles.summary: Fagner Lima era pastor em uma igreja evangélica de Buriti Alegre e era conhecido pela sua dedicação à esposa e ao único filho. Bombeiros ainda buscam o corpo do menino de 4 anos.
articles.body:
O pai que morreu depois de cair junto com o filho no Lago das Brisas , em Buriti Alegre , no sul de Goiás, era pastor de uma igreja evangélica e conhecido pelo amor à família. Fagner de Lima Oliveira, de 32 anos, se afogou após o barco em que ele e o menino de 4 anos estavam perder o controle, de acordo com o Corpo de Bombeiros. O corpo do garoto ainda está sendo procurado pelos militares.

Nas redes sociais, a esposa dele e mãe do menino, Jaqueline Oliveira, costuma compartilhar momentos da família reunida. No dia 19 de julho, ela divulgou um vídeo, em seu perfil do Instagram, em que o filho aparece brincando à beira de um lago, junto com outra criança. Dias antes, publicou momentos de passeios com ele e o esposo.

Jaqueline e Fagner também se declaravam um ao outro publicamente. Uma semana antes do acidente no lago, ela publicou um vídeo mostrando mudança no visual, em um salão de beleza,. Fagner comentou: "Simplesmente bela!", acompanhado de um emoji apaixonado.

Fagner Lima e a esposa Jaqueline Oliveira costumavam se declarar um ao outro nas redes sociais — Foto: Reprodução/Perfil do Instagram de Jaqueline Oliveira

Jaqueline também compartilhava momentos em que o marido estava pregando no púlpito da igreja, a Assembleia de Deus Centro-Norte de Corumbazul, um povoado turístico de Buriti Alegre.

Em entrevista ao g1 , Tays França, cunhada de Fagner, disse que a irmã dela, esposa dele, está "completamente derrotada".

Sobre o cunhado, Tays o definiu como um "homem incrível".

"Um super pai. Homem de Deus. Um homem de coração gigante", afirmou.

Tays também homenageou o único sobrinho. "Deus levou um menino lindo, inteligente. Era uma criança que se espelhava no pai, que era um grande homem de Deus", relatou.

Segundo Tays, a família é de Aparecida de Goiânia , mas mora em Buriti há cerca de cinco anos.

Fagner Lima morreu após cair no Lago das Brisas, em Buriti Alegre, junto com o filho de 4 anos — Foto: Reprodução/Perfil do Instagram de Jaqueline Oliveira

O acidente aconteceu no final da tarde de sexta-feira (18). Segundo o Corpo de Bombeiros, pai e filho caíram e, de acordo com relatos de testemunhas, logo submergiram. Os dois estavam sem coletes salva-vidas.

O corpo de Fagner foi encontrado pelos militares na manhã de sábado (19) . As buscas pelo corpo do menino continuam. Os trabalhos contam com o apoio de mergulhadores do Corpo de Bombeiros enviados de Itumbiara e Goiânia .

articles.title: C&A é condenada a indenizar gestante que trabalhava em pé | G1
articles.standfirst: Trabalhadora passava grande parte da jornada de trabalho em pé por falta de assentos na loja. A empresa também é acusada de descontar do salário dela a parcela de consignado e não repassar o dinheiro ao banco.
articles.summary: Justiça condena C&A a indenizar gestante que trabalhava em pé e teve descontos de consignado retidos, reconhecendo a rescisão indireta do contrato de trabalho da operadora de caixa.
articles.body:
Funcionária trabalhava como operadora de caixa na C&A de Praia Grande — Foto: Reprodução/Redes sociais

A Justiça do Trabalho de Praia Grande , no litoral de São Paulo, reconheceu a rescisão indireta de uma funcionária da C&A Modas que passava grande parte da jornada de trabalho em pé por falta de assentos e também teve descontos indevidos na folha de pagamento . A decisão ainda condenou a empresa a indenizar a profissional por danos morais.

A sentença publicada pela 1ª Vara do Trabalho de Praia Grande condenou a companhia a pagar R$ 18 mil à ex-funcionária, sendo R$ 7 mil somente por danos morais e o restante de direitos trabalhistas como FGTS, 13º proporcional, férias, entre outros.

🔎 A rescisão indireta ocorre quando o trabalhador pede a saída do emprego por culpa do empregador que descumpriu a lei ou o contrato. A situação é popularmente conhecida como “justa causa” aplicada ao patrão.

Em nota, a C&A informou que não comenta processos judiciais em andamento, mas reforça o compromisso com a ética, a integridade e a promoção de um ambiente pautado pelo respeito e pela dignidade de todas as pessoas.

A mulher trabalhava como operadora de caixa na unidade da C&A em um shopping na cidade e, segundo a defesa, permanecia em pé durante praticamente toda a jornada de trabalho , inclusive no período de gestação.

Ela deu à luz em março de 2026 e continuou tendo parcelas de um empréstimo consignado descontadas do salário durante a licença-maternidade. No entanto, a mulher foi surpreendida pela instituição financeira onde havia feito o empréstimo com uma cobrança extrajudicial que informava o atraso de duas parcelas.

Confrontada pela funcionária, a C&A não comprovou o repasse do dinheiro à instituição financeira responsável pelo empréstimo. A profissional entrou com uma ação trabalhista pedindo rescisão indireta e indenização por danos morais.

Durante a audiência de instrução, testemunhas da trabalhadora e da empresa confirmaram que havia apenas dois assentos para um grupo grande de funcionários.

O juiz Francisco Charles Florentino de Sousa reconheceu a rescisão indireta considerando as condições de trabalho ofertadas e as parcelas descontadas do salário da mulher. Ele registrou como "incontroverso", ou seja, incontestável, que a empresa reteve os valores e concluiu que a C&A não conseguiu demonstrar o repasse ao banco, apesar de prazo judicial para isso.

O advogado Danillo de Oliveira Britto, que representa a trabalhadora, contou que recebeu a sentença com o "sentimento de dever cumprido".

"Entendo que a Justiça cumpriu seu papel fundamental ao restabelecer o equilíbrio entre as partes e garantir o respeito aos direitos essenciais. A decisão serve, ainda, como um importante alerta sobre a necessidade de preservação da dignidade, da saúde e da integridade do trabalhador no ambiente de trabalho", informou.

articles.title: Ela transformou um picolé em um negócio de R$ 1,4 milhão | G1
articles.standfirst: Grávida da segunda filha e sem trabalho, Thayany dos Santos começou produzindo 100 picolés em casa. Hoje, com dez funcionários, fabrica até 20 mil unidades por mês no Recife.
articles.summary: Grávida da segunda filha e sem trabalho, Thayany dos Santos começou produzindo 100 picolés em casa. Hoje, com dez funcionários, fabrica até 20 mil unidades por mês no Recife.
articles.body:
Em 2017, a vida colocou Thayany dos Santos diante de uma encruzilhada. Grávida da segunda filha e desempregada, ela buscava uma forma de complementar a renda quando recebeu uma sugestão de uma prima: vender picolés.

O que parecia uma alternativa temporária acabou se tornando um negócio que transformaria sua trajetória profissional e pessoal.

Sem experiência na produção de sorvetes, Thayany procurou ajuda de uma amiga que já dominava a técnica. Os primeiros ingredientes vieram de uma doação da madrasta, que ofereceu leite condensado, creme de leite, leite em pó e chocolate para que ela pudesse fazer os testes iniciais.

"Eu ganhei leite condensado, creme de leite, leite em pó e chocolate", relembra a empreendedora. Com cerca de 100 unidades produzidas e vendidas a R$ 3 cada, nasceu o embrião da marca que hoje está consolidada no Recife .

Os desafios não demoraram a aparecer. O liquidificador doméstico usado na produção não resistiu ao aumento da demanda.

Segundo a empreendedora, pelo menos cinco aparelhos quebraram durante os primeiros anos da operação. Ainda assim, ela continuou investindo no negócio, aprimorando receitas e conquistando clientes.

A empresa atravessou momentos difíceis, especialmente durante a pandemia. Foi nesse período que Thayany ganhou um aliado importante: Fellipe Miguel, hoje marido e sócio.

Empreender era um sonho antigo dele, que enxergou potencial no negócio e decidiu contribuir para o crescimento da marca.

De desempregada a dona de fábrica: empreendedora fatura R$ 1,4 milhão por ano com picolés gourmet — Foto: Reprodução/PEGN

Em vez de competir apenas pelo preço, Thayany apostou na diferenciação. Inspirada em sobremesas tradicionais, criou sabores como pavê, pudim e cheesecake de frutas vermelhas.

O cuidado também se estendeu às embalagens, que passaram a ser personalizadas com a identidade da marca após um investimento de R$ 3 mil.

A estratégia ajudou a fortalecer a percepção de valor do produto. Atualmente, a empresa conta com mais de 30 sabores e produz entre 18 mil e 20 mil picolés por mês.

O negócio gera emprego para dez pessoas, sendo sete mulheres que atuam na fábrica em diferentes etapas da produção. Para Thayany, a unidade fabril é o coração da empresa. A qualidade dos produtos também abriu portas para novos mercados.

Um dos momentos mais marcantes ocorreu quando a marca foi contratada para fornecer picolés para a festa do filho do cantor João Gomes, após ser encontrada nas redes sociais pela família do artista.

"A mulher do João Gomes me achou na rede social, mandou mensagem e me contratou. Foi surreal", afirma a empresária.

Hoje, a empresa registra faturamento anual de R$ 1,4 milhão e opera em uma loja com mais de 100 metros quadrados . Agora, o próximo objetivo é construir uma indústria própria, planejada para ampliar a capacidade produtiva e profissionalizar ainda mais os processos.

O desafio, segundo especialistas, é crescer mantendo a qualidade que conquistou os clientes.

Durante o programa, a chef confeiteira e empresária Carole Crema aconselhou Thayany a investir na padronização das receitas e na criação de fichas técnicas detalhadas para garantir que o produto mantenha as mesmas características à medida que a empresa se expande.

Para a empreendedora, o caminho percorrido até aqui já representa uma vitória. "O picolé mudou a minha vida. Uma coisa tão simples, mas feita com amor, dedicação e propósito", resume Thayany dos Santos.

De uma produção feita com equipamentos domésticos a uma operação capaz de vender milhares de unidades por mês, ela resume a trajetória em uma frase simples: "O picolé mudou a minha vida".

Segundo dados da Associação Brasileira das Indústrias e do Setor de Sorvetes (ABIS), 92% das empresas do setor de sorvetes no Brasil são micro e pequenas empresas, cenário que reforça o potencial de histórias como a de Thayany.

articles.summary: O nome dele é Arthur Alves Santos, mas pode ser chamado de “Arthurzinho” ou de “Seu Chico”. O primo Vitor Alves mostra a rotina com o menino e avó, de 91 anos, em Juazeiro do Norte
articles.body:
A máxima “uma imagem vale mais que mil palavras” traduz bem a relação do público com o pequeno Arthur Alves Santos, de 2 anos. Os vídeos, publicados pelo primo Vitor Alves, viralizaram nas redes sociais mesmo sem o menino dizer uma única palavra . O que encanta mesmo é o jeito do pequeno, que parece um “senhorzinho” meio vaqueiro, meio agricultor, em pleno sertão do Ceará .

O chapéu de couro marrom claro, ou então de palha, na cabeça contrasta perfeitamente com o chinelinho de tiras, que impedem os pés de escapar. Abaixo do chapéu, as bochechas contrastam com o semblante fechado, “sem dar moral pra ninguém”, como se diz no Ceará. O jeito do “Arthurzinho”, apelido carinhoso do menino, rendeu-lhe também mais uma alcunha: “Seu Chico” .

Quem publica os vídeos é Vitor, de 29 anos, primo de segundo grau do pequeno “pseudoidoso”. Os vídeos de Vitor seguem o roteiro mais simples possível: ele liga a câmera e filma a própria rotina. Tudo começou com a avó, a “Vovó Joaninha” . Arthur chegou depois e encantou os quase 200 mil seguidores do jovem.

Vitor mora na comunidade Sítio Leite, zona rural de Juazeiro do Norte , no Cariri do estado, a cerca de 500 km de Fortaleza. Na mesma comunidade, moram Arthur e a mãe, em outra casa. No localidade ao lado, mora Joana Coelho Ferreira, de 91 anos — a Vovó Joaninha.

“Um dia, eu gravando minha avó, ele apareceu aleatoriamente no vídeo. Daí, muita gente começou a mandar mensagem perguntando quem era ele, que ele parecia um senhorzinho, parecia um velhinho de idade. E eu comecei a gravar ele porque o pessoal achava que ele era um meme. E os vídeos dele viralizaram”, explicou Vitor.

Arthurzinho, apelidado de "Seu Chico", diverte nas redes sociais com jeito de idoso do interior do Ceará. — Foto: Redes sociais/Reprodução

Vitor comentou que muitas pessoas o questionam se ele pede para que Arthur assuma a pose “marrenta” durante os vídeos, mas ele sempre responde que aquele é o jeito espontâneo da criança.

“É só aquele jeito espontâneo dele, de senhorzinho. A gente bota só um chapéuzinho nele para ele passear pelo sítio da avó e vira esse meme que está aí. Ele é ‘fechadão’, ele parece um senhor. Não dá moral a ninguém”, explicou.

Vitor não sabe explicar com exatidão porque o Arturzinho tem essa postura, mas acredita que pode até estar ligado à genética. “O avô dele também é exatamente igual ele. O pai da mãe dele. Ele é muito ‘fechadão’. Então a gente conversa que talvez ele tenha puxado o avô”, considerou o criador de conteúdo.

Vitor mostra a rotina com Arhurzinho e a Vovó Joaninha em Juazeiro do Norte, no Ceará. — Foto: Redes sociais/Reprodução

Antes de gravar vídeos com Arthur, Vitor já costumava filmar a rotina com a avó, que também tem um jeito espontâneo que diverte a internet, devido às respostas “curtas e grossas”.

“Ela tem o jeitão dela, sempre com alguma resposta. [Quando eu postava] eu via que tinha muita resposta no Instagram. O pessoal pedia: ‘faz um Instagram pra tua avó’”, lembrou Vitor.

“A gente não costuma 'criar conteúdo'. Eu apenas chego, ligo minha câmera, gravo a rotina normal de minha avó, e ela é aquela pessoa. Tanto pessoalmente, quanto fora das câmeras”, explicou.

As publicações com a avó começaram após Vitor sofrer um acidente de motocicleta e ficar três meses afastado do trabalho; anteriormente ele era funcionário de um supermercado no Centro de Juazeiro do Norte. Em recuperação, ele acabou aumentando a convivência com a avó.

A maioria dos vídeos com a Vovó Joaninha e o Seu Chico, inclusive, é gravado no sítio onde a aposentada mora.

“Geralmente a casa da minha avó é cheia de gente direto. Eu chego lá pela parte da manhã, quando ele [Arthur] não está no colégio, a mãe dele está lá com ele. Ele fica lá, conversando com a minha avó, vai tomar café com a mãe dele lá. É quando eu chego, filmando ele e vovó”, disse Vitor.

articles.title: An Ohio farmer watched gullies repeatedly cut through his family's 700-acre farm and decided to change how he worked the land; decades later, the family operation has grown to 8,000 acres while becoming a conservation showcase
articles.summary: US News: For Bill Kellogg, conservation did not begin with a government program, a sustainability label or a push for recognition. It began with gullies. Watch.
articles.body: For Bill Kellogg, conservation did not begin with a government program, a sustainability label or a push for recognition. It began with gullies. Watching water repeatedly carve through his family’s rolling farmland convinced him that the way the ground was being worked had to change. What followed was a decades-long effort to protect the soil while building a larger, more efficient and profitable farm. Scroll down to read the details.From erosion control to precision farmingAccording to a report by Farm Progress, Kellogg’s original 700-acre operation has expanded to about 8,000 acres, with 1,800 acres owned and the remainder rented. Along the way, conservation evolved from grass waterways and water and sediment control basins into a much broader system. Today, the Hardin County farm uses grid soil testing, no-till and strip-till practices, precision nutrient management, cover crops, buffer strips, subsurface drainage, pollinator habitat and about 60 acres of waterways.The shift toward precision agriculture accelerated when Bill’s son, Shane, became involved in the operation. Grid soil sampling began in 1999, giving the family a clearer picture of how nutrients were moving through their fields and how the soil responded to management decisions.Strip-till eventually became a particularly visible part of the farm’s approach. Instead of broadcasting fertilizer across an entire field, the Kelloggs began banding nutrients where crops could access them more efficiently. The approach has helped reduce fertilizer use while maintaining or improving yields, states the online report.Adapting instead of following a formulaThe Kelloggs do not treat conservation as a one-size-fits-all system. Cover crops, for example, are used selectively, particularly on rolling ground where they can provide greater erosion protection. The farm also is not strictly no-till. Tillage generally remains shallow, rarely going beyond two inches except when drainage or leveling work requires deeper disturbance, and that flexibility extends to fertilizer decisions. With phosphate prices expected to rise above $900 per ton, the family is reconsidering chicken litter as a nutrient source, adds the Farm Progress report. The farm used the material 15 to 20 years ago and is now examining whether bringing it back could make economic sense.A farm built through difficult timesThe Kellogg story is also one of persistence. He began farming at 14 after his father left agriculture to care for his ill wife. By his senior year of high school, Bill was managing 700 acres, much of it through relationships with older farmers in the community. The farm survived the severe agricultural crisis of the early 1980s, when Bill faced foreclosure and sold possessions to keep the operation afloat. A combination of family help and a shrewd investment in payment-in-kind certificates helped him emerge from the debt crisis, states the report. Those experiences shaped a straightforward financial philosophy: profitability matters alongside stewardship. And that principle remains central as Shane manages the farm’s day-to-day operations and works to expand what his father built.Conservation as a family legacyThe Kelloggs’ conservation work gained a wider audience after they joined a Farm Bureau and Natural Resources Conservation Service demonstration project following the 2014 Toledo water crisis. The family later became involved with H2Ohio and has opened its farm to thousands of visitors, including students, officials and journalists.Their efforts recently earned the family the Ohio Conservation Farm Family Award. The farm now involves multiple generations, with Bill, Shane, Jacinta Burd and their families contributing to its future.Images Courtesy: Farm ProgressCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Massive' drone attack on Moscow region sees Ukraine hit oil refinery
articles.summary: Moscow's mayor says 450 drones were downed during the "unprecedented attack", in which two people died.
articles.body:
At least two people have been killed and six injured in a "massive" overnight Ukrainian drone attack on the Moscow region, Governor Andrei Vorobyev has said.

Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 450 drones heading for the capital had been shot down in what he called an "unprecedented attack". The city's main oil refinery was damaged and several homes were set ablaze.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed Kyiv had hit a "key" Russian oil facility and a logistics site in the region, representing "billions of dollars that sustain the war machine".

Ukrainian officials meanwhile said nine people, including three children, had been killed in Russian attacks in the Kyiv and Sumy regions on Saturday.

The overnight attack is thought to be among the largest drone attacks on the Moscow region since the war began.

Russia and Ukraine have recently intensified their strikes, targeting energy-generating and transport facilities, as well as major logistics hubs.

A 44-year-old woman was killed in Sofyino on Sunday after a drone hit a three-storey residential building, regional head Vorobyev said. Another five people - including two children - were injured.

An elderly man died after a private house was hit in the Orekhovo-Zuevo district, Vorobyev added.

Videos have emerged on social media appearing to show explosions in the night skies above Moscow, and a burning warehouse. The footage has not been verified by the BBC.

Mayor Sobyanin said a drone had struck a building near one of the capital's boulevards and the oil refinery - where Ukrainian military officials said three key units had been damaged.

The site supplies more than a third of the Moscow region's fuel, according to the defence ministry in Kyiv, and some of its petrol, diesel and aviation fuel go to Russia's military.

Ukraine's defence minister said attacking such facilities "directly undermines the enemy's ability to continue its war of aggression and supply its military formations".

Sobyanin said the major attack was "an attempt to disrupt" Russia's parliamentary election, which was in its third day on Sunday. The vote is tightly controlled by the Kremlin and has been dismissed by critics as neither free, fair nor transparent.

Russian state media reported that an election official was one of two people killed by a drone attack on a bus in a Moscow-controlled part of Kherson in Ukraine on Sunday, citing the head of Russia's election commission.

Meanwhile, Moscow's biggest airport Sheremetyevo warned passengers "temporary restrictions" were in place overnight, while at the capital's Vnukovo airport all arrivals and departures were halted. Restrictions at both airports were lifted by Sunday morning but each warned some flights may still be delayed.

It comes after a mother and her two small children, a boy and a girl, were killed in a Russian attack in the city of Fastiv, Kyiv on Sautrday, according to regional head Tymur Tkachenko.

He later said a child injured in a separate attack in Vyshhorod, north of Kyiv, had also died in hospital.

In the north-eastern Sumy region, four people were killed when a Russian drone hit the car they were travelling in, top local official Oleh Hryhorov said.

Russia also struck a monastery in the Kherson region with a drone on Saturday, Zelensky said, killing one member of the clergy and injuring four others.

Both Russia and Ukraine have continued to hit energy infrastructure targets in the past week, despite US President Donald Trump claiming on social media that the two sides had agreed not to do so.

Trump signed a sanctions bill on Friday that targets Russia's economy by implementing tariffs on the biggest buyers of the country's oil and gas which include China and India.

The US legislation gives the US president powers to impose 100% tariffs on major purchasers of Russian energy.

Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

articles.title: Plans to replace Chiltern museum's 'Horrible Histories' roundhouse
articles.summary: The new roundhouse will be historically accurate, including a floor made of "chalk and cheese".
articles.body:
An open-air museum is looking to build a new replica Iron Age roundhouse to replace its current one, which has featured in the BBC's Horrible Histories comedy series.

The Chiltern Open Air Museum in Chalfont St Giles, Buckinghamshire, said the new roundhouse would be historically accurate, including a floor made of "chalk and cheese" - an early form of concrete .

Learning manager for the museum, Jon Gibson, said the current roundhouse gave the 12,000 schoolchildren who visited every year "a real sense of what life was like" in ancient times.

About £10,500 has been raised so far for its replacement, with the attraction setting a £50,000 fundraising target.

The Horrible Histories franchise started out as a series of books and later became a popular CBBC show, enjoyed by children and adults for its dark humour and surreal parodies.

The existing roundhouse featured in the show in 2009 but the structure is now 30 years old and needs to be replaced, with the museum adding that roundhouses in the Iron Age were not built to last forever.

The museum is planning to base the new roundhouse on the most up-to-date archaeological research.

The new structure will have a roof made of cereal straw, similar to that seen in local Iron Age sites.

It will also have naturally curved timbers which will be set into the ground, and connected with wooden nails to make arches.

The walls will be made of hazel and brushwood wattle and daub, and will be painted with designs based on local pottery, metalwork and other Iron Age artefacts.

The "chalk and cheese" floor will also include cheese curds, known as casein, which when mixed with the chalk creates a natural reaction that sets hard.

Throughout construction, visitors will be able to watch the roundhouse take shape and learn about the materials, techniques and skills involved.

Gibson said schoolchildren were "always amazed at how dark it is inside" the current roundhouse, "and how warm the fire is".

"They go home slightly grubby, smelling of wood smoke, having had a fantastic day," he added.

articles.title: Why bookshops are booming in the TikTok age
articles.summary: Proprietors explain why more independent bookshops are springing up in our towns and cities.
articles.body:
Opening your own book shop might be a lofty daydream for some bookworms looking to escape their 9-5, but more and more people are making it a reality.

According to the Booksellers Association, the number of independent book shops in the UK and Ireland is now at its highest level since 2012, with 1,086 stores in 2025 - up from a record low of 867 in 2016.

But what is the reality of life as a small bookseller, competing with Amazon, finding new customers, and actually trying to make a profit?

Sally Flint, 57, opened The Book Stop in Brigg, North Lincolnshire, just six weeks ago.

So far, the "dream" move is living up to her expectations, but it has not been without its challenges.

"It's brilliant. It's just like it's Christmas Day every day, because you're just with other people who love books and love reading," she says.

However, to make her dream possible, Sally is working up to 14 hours a day.

She describes her first foray into bookselling as a "steep learning curve", but says she is having "lots of fun along the way".

Georgina Wilson, 47, opened Clutterbooks in the East Yorkshire seaside town of Hornsea in November 2025.

She "tested the market" in the local community, running a bookshop market stall and book club before taking the plunge when a vacant unit came up for rent.

Georgina describes the move into bookselling from early years education as "brilliant", and says the shop has been "very well received" by local residents, but she also had a lot to learn about running a retail business.

Similar to Sally, Georgina found the start of her bookselling journey "overwhelming" when faced with selecting stock for the shop.

Unlike Sally and Georgina, it was never Sleaford resident Shannon Hanson's dream to own a book shop.

But after starting a local book club, she leapt at the chance to rent a space in the Lincolnshire town.

Opening Chapter & Page Books in Bristol Arcade in August, the 35-year-old says it has been a "baptism of fire".

Shannon juggles her day job as a part-time nurse with running the bookshop. She is assisted by volunteers.

She hopes the bookshop will eventually earn her a living.

While these three booksellers are all enjoying their first leap into bookshop ownership, others have found retail conditions challenging.

One Bristol bookshop recently started a crowd funding campaign to help stay afloat, while another in Clitheroe blamed high rents for the closure of his bookshop.

While reading may have once been seen as a hobby for those in their later years, some research suggests a resurgence in book buying is being driven by a younger audience .

A recent report from Public First, with additional research from EY, found that in 2025 TikTok helped generate £175m in consumer spending on books.

The research also found that nearly half of young adult readers who use TikTok (48%) said they had bought a book after seeing it on the platform.

Sally said she had noticed young people buying items "to have on their shelves, kind of like a trophy book", after initially reading them on an e-reader.

Shannon, who described herself as a "sucker for the social media aspect of books", said she believes that the "social aspect of book reading", such as sharing photographs of your book shelves, or posting reviews online, has driven the resurgence in the popularity of reading.

Shannon thinks people are also coming into bookshops looking for connection rather than products.

She says: "They [bookshops] are not just a brick and mortar shop to sell books. They're actually a community and they're creating events for people that love these types of books."

Sally has taken this further at her bookshop, running other community clubs alongside book clubs, including a regular crochet group and other "special" events, including book signings.

Shannon also holds special events at her book shop, celebrating the release of Gruffalo Granny by Julia Donaldson, with a special visit from the beast himself. Dozens of local children attended.

Georgina now runs eight book clubs a month, which she says has created "a really nice customer base and a really nice sort of community feel to the shop".

They range from clubs for young people, including a home education group for those who are home-schooled, as well as regular groups for adults.

Community is an important aspect of reading for book lover Ian Dixon, 54, from Hull.

He bought more than 550 physical copies of books last year, many of them from independent shops.

"I love visiting bookshops. They're my happy place. Honestly, if I'm ever feeling a bit fed up with myself, I just go out, find a bookshop and I just browse. I could sit in there for hours," he says.

The social aspect is also important for Ian, who cannot work due to living with uncontrollable epileptic seizures. He attends several Hull Silent Book Club events every week.

Though it is still early in Sally, Georgina and Shannon's book selling journeys, they are optimistic that the individuality of their stores can help secure long-term customers.

articles.title: Social media addiction affecting older people, BBC hears
articles.summary: From "endless scroll" to beating loneliness, experts and users discuss how boomers use social media.
articles.body:
"It is addictive," says 62-year-old Tracie from West Sussex. "I spend far too much time on my phone.

"I pick it up without realising a lot of the time... and before I know it, I've lost complete track of time idly scrolling."

Tracie is one of more than 50% of adults aged over 55 who use social media at least once a week, according to a 2026 YouGov poll .

"It's an epidemic," she said. "We are addicted to the scroll."

Having used social media during the lockdown to entertain herself, Tracie said she has since limited her usage - even deleting some platforms from her phone.

"I don't think it's good for you," she said.

"Social media fills your head so you've got no headspace for anything that's relevant or important.

"You miss so much as a parent or a grandparent when you're on your phone all the time. You are not in that moment."

Speaking to the BBC as the government works on plans to ban social media usage for children under 16, Tracie said it was important older people set an example.

"It's not just about the young - it's consuming for all ages," she said.

"It's all well and good paying attention to [how] kids [use their phone], but older people need to be mindful too.

"I don't think there is enough emphasis on the role modelling that we're doing for our grandchildren and children.

David Harley, a University of Brighton cyberpsychology lecturer and researcher, said early concerns used to focus on whether or not older people would be able to use digital technologies, like social media.

While still an issue, he said attention was now on the potential harms of their usage.

"In the early days of social media," Harley explained. "The creation of content and participatory interactive stuff was much more prominent.

"As time's gone on, that's become less and less dominant. Now there's a lot more passive consumption and algorithmic content... that grabs attention."

This has fed addiction and other problematic behaviours, he said.

Though Harley said all age groups were susceptible, he told the BBC more research needed to be done into the impacts on older people.

Still, researchers have also pointed to benefits of this group using social media.

Brigitte Stangl, an associate professor and digital expert at the University of Surrey, told the BBC it can be very effective in reducing loneliness in older people.

"Being online can get rid of issues around mobility or [accessing] transport" that particularly affect this demographic, she explained.

Stangl said social media was able to give older people "real connections" they may not have been able to maintain before the internet, especially if their families were dispersed and scattered around the globe.

She suggested it could also potentially help reduce cognitive decline in old age.

Kerri Hedley-Cheney, a 61-year-old from Worthing in West Sussex, said that without social media she would have lost touch with many people in her life.

"That's been an absolutely beautiful thing," she said.

Hedley-Cheney, an actress, added social media had allowed her to be part of acting groups where they made connections and supported one another.

But she added: "The flip side of that is that you waste hours when you should be... focusing on what needs to be done.

"The floors don't get hoovered by finding out what Janice from accounts is doing.

She also said social media usage had decreased her concentration span - an effect normally associated with younger people.

"Years ago it was much stronger - now it's about 10 seconds," she said.

When asked if she would like to use social media less, Hedley-Cheney said "no".

She added: "It's a fantastic tool we have at our fingertips for reaching people, finding advice on things and getting help if you need it."

Stangl said the key thing was how social media was used.

"We need to differentiate between this going down the rabbit hole of non-stop scrolling - which we know impacts our brains negatively - compared to using [social media] in a purposeful, useful and meaningful way.

"There are groups of older adults who are very good with everything online and technology... and there are definitely others at risk," she said.

articles.title: Poorer North East and Cumbria families missing out on food help
articles.summary: Figures show as few as 64% of eligible families are claiming NHS money to buy milk, fruit and veg.
articles.body:
Charities are warning that thousands of low income families are missing out on money they are eligible to claim to buy fresh fruit, vegetables, and milk.

Families earning less than £400 a week are entitled to weekly NHS Health Start payments including pregnant women and those with children under four years old who are entitled to £4.65 a week.

Figures found take-up of the scheme is as low as 64% in some parts of the North East and Cumbria.

Newcastle-based charity Feeding Britain said hikes in food prices meant "every layer of protection possible" was needed for families on the lowest incomes. The government has been approached for comment.

Amelia, from Sunderland, has a two-year-old son and does not qualify for the scheme, but said she understood the struggle families face.

"It's expensive to feed the whole family. It's getting ridiculous really. It's not just food, it's the nappies and wipes and days out."

She said she tries to batch cook to save money and eat the same meals as her son.

Amy, a working mother with a toddler, said: "He was on formula and it was expensive for the tins. They never had offers or promotions."

She said she often eats less so her son can have more food.

Families with a baby under 12 months old can claim £9.30 a week as part of the NHS Health Start scheme.

However, figures suggest thousands of eligible families have not enrolled.

The latest NHS figures on the take-up are from 2022.

Redcar and Cleveland Council had the highest enrolment - 87% of entitled families were claiming the weekly payments.

In the former Eden Council area, only 64% of those eligible were enrolled and in the former Copeland Council area, take-up was 68%.

In Sunderland and Stockton, 81% of eligible families were enrolled.

Take-up was lower in Newcastle and Middlesbrough, where just 77% of those entitled to payments received them.

Across the region that meant 6,149 eligible families were missing out.

Penny Walters works for Feeding Britain which supports some of the most deprived families in the North East.

She said Healthy Start payments were not increasing in line with inflation.

"£4.65 - what can you buy with that?" she said.

"If you've got a baby you get £9.30 and you can buy one tin of formula with that.

"But how many tins have you got to go through a week with a baby? It's worthless."

She said professionals were still finding stark levels of poverty in the region, including a malnourished baby admitted to hospital in Newcastle.

"The only thing the mam could afford to give the baby was sugar water," she said.

"That's not right. We're not in Dickensian England. Where was the support? Why is this happening?"

Several national charities are calling for the Healthy Start scheme to be updated, including Sustain, The Food Foundation, and Feeding Britain.

Newcastle-based Feeding Britain director Andrew Forsey said: "Given the increases in food prices that are coming our way in the months ahead we need every layer of protection possible for families on the lowest incomes."

He said the government should make Healthy Start an auto-enrollment scheme for eligible families.

"The government can use the data and the technology at its disposal to register parents automatically, just to lift some of the burden off parents' shoulders," he said.

Labour MP for South Shields, Emma Lewell, said she had been campaigning to try and ensure the allocated money does not return to the Treasury if unclaimed.

"It just feels like such a no brainer," she said.

"The money is there, the government have it, it's not going to the people who need it and there's things we can do to make sure it does, but they're not being done.

Charities are also calling on the Department for Health and Social Care to release updated figures on enrollment on the scheme.

The NHS stopped publishing data in January 2023 due to an inaccuracy that was discovered and this has not since been rectified.

It means charities and local authorities cannot track who might be missing out.

The department has been approached for comment.

articles.title: When did grey squirrels start posing a threat to reds in the UK?
articles.summary: A pair of grey squirrels was reportedly brought to the United Kingdom by a Cheshire banker in 1876.
articles.body:
Endangered red squirrel populations have plummeted from about 3.5 million to less than 300,000 in the UK, with their grey-haired rivals continuing to thrive.

But when exactly did the squirrel stand-off begin and how bad has the situation become?

In England, the situation is particularly dire for reds.

The Woodland Trust reckons there are only 39,000 of them left, while the Save Our Reds campaign thinks just 15,000 remain, including in conservation areas such as Formby on Merseyside.

In stark contrast, since their introduction from North America in the 19th Century, greys have thrived at the expense of their distant cousins, which compete for habitats and carry lethal viruses.

The first verifiable importation of greys is widely understood to have come 150 years ago, when a Victorian banker named Thomas V. Brocklehurst is said to have released a pair of greys into Henbury Park, near Macclesfield in Cheshire, that he had brought back from a business trip to the United States.

The rest, they say, is history and nobody back then would have realised the unintended lasting consequences of his actions.

According to Graham Paskett from the Red Squirrel Survival Trust, there are now between 2.5 million and 2.7 million greys in the UK.

Jackie Foott, from the British Red Squirrel conservation group, told the BBC that reds and greys cannot coexist in the same location and that to protect the reds you have to "get rid of the greys - we realised that a while ago".

She explained: "The grey squirrel is a pest, non-native, invasive species.

"People don't realise just how much damage they are doing to trees, crops and properties - they cause at least £40m damage to forests and forestry services each year."

But why can reds and greys not live cheek by jowl?

"Greys outcompete reds for habitat and food - they don't actually physically attack them but they do bother them," said Foott.

"Secondly, greys have squirrel pox - it doesn't affect them but they transmit it to red squirrels and it's fatal for them. It's a horrible disease and causes them ulcers and blindness."

"Fertility control isn't available now - and has the effect of affecting other species, including reds," said Foott. "Gene therapy is probably at least 10 years away.

"For now, the only way is lethal control - by shooting or trapping."

Paskett, though, thinks there could be an effective additional way to control grey squirrel numbers within the next five years.

He said the Red Squirrel Survival Trust was jointly funding a field trial by the government's Animal and Plant Health Agency.

Beginning "later this year or early next year" Paskett said his organisation had "developed the means to deliver oral contraceptives to grey squirrels using a 'hopper' which sees the squirrel lift up a lid" to access them.

Because greys typically weigh 500g - approximately twice that of reds, only they can access the contraceptive.

If the field trial is successful, Paskett hopes landowners and forest rangers will be able to sign up to the scheme.

For now, though, Foott said shooting and trapping were the main options.

However, she said: "The reintroduction of pine martens can help. Because they are a native species in the UK, they evolved together with red squirrels.

"They do eat red squirrels but the reds know to quickly get out of their way and will send out the alarm signal to the rest of the colony.

"The greys are a little bit stupid and will say 'hello, I haven't seen you before' and the pine marten will get them!"

When asked about the grey squirrels' UK origin story, Foott said: "Nobody really knows - there are several records but it doesn't really matter."

So why were greys imported in the first place?

Foott said: "Somebody said 'Wouldn't they look cute running around my garden?'

More than a century later, she said experienced British Red Squirrel volunteers were now working with farmers and landowners to control grey squirrel populations near red colonies.

In May, a spokesperson for the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said the government was protecting endangered red squirrels by tackling the threat of non-native grey squirrels.

articles.title: Cloud-like sculptures installed in new Oxford North public park
articles.summary: The Length of a Moment artworks sit in the new public park at the Oxford North development.
articles.body:
A series of cloud-like sculptures have been unveiled at a site that will eventually be home to laboratories, offices, a park and hundreds of homes.

The Length of a Moment artworks sit in the new public park at the Oxford North development - best known in the local area for the large red-roofed structure at its heart .

The trio of bronze sculptures depict the plume of scent a flower releases into the air as a moth searches for its nectar.

Artist Alexandra Daisy Ginsberg said the works - which are more than two metres (6.5ft) tall - "celebrate the part every living creature plays in the world we share".

"I wanted to give one of the slightest, most fleeting exchanges a form we can witness, and to invite the curiosity and empathy that come from really looking," she explained.

"To see the sculptures in the meadow they belong to, surrounded by the wildlife they are really about, is the best place this work could be."

Oxford North is based on 64 acres of land within the city's northern boundary - near to Peartree Roundabout and the A34.

It is from the new recreation ground, Canalside Park, that the three bronze sculptures now rise.

Ginsberg used computer modelling to simulate the natural occurrence between flowers and months - which is invisible to the human eye.

"I hope people slow down... and feel something of what it might be like to experience the world the way a moth does," she said.

Victoria Collett, development director of Thomas White Oxford, the firm behind the new park, said the artwork was a "beautiful expression" of the "ambition" of Oxford North.

"An artwork that sits lightly within the landscape while offering something profound for those who encounter it," she said.

Oxford City Council leader Susan Brown, who unveiled the sculptures, said public art "always has an important role to play" in the city.

"I'm delighted that this work will be here for residents, visitors and future generations to discover and enjoy," she added.

articles.title: A California retiree began picking up litter alone on daily walks in 2020; six years later, her volunteer group has removed about 750,000 pounds of trash and now organises valley-wide cleanups
articles.summary: US News: Life always has a purpose, and the fun part is that you get to decide it. You can spend a fine morning sleeping through it or volunteering your time f.
articles.body: Life always has a purpose, and the fun part is that you get to decide it. You can spend a fine morning sleeping through it or volunteering your time for a purpose. For Jill Mather her retirement wasn't going as planned. After decades of working 80-hour weeks in the restaurant business, she had dreamt of travelling, relaxing and spending time with old friends. But soon, COVID-19 struck and Jill was itching to do something.“I can take a long walk at least,” she told herself one morning, and headed out to stroll 4 miles through her San Fernando neighbourhood. She did it again the next day, but as she walked block after block, she noticed there was litter everywhere — cans, bottles and trash. The next morning she grabbed numerous plastic grocery bags and headed out on her walk with a renewed purpose. “That’s a great idea,” neighbours called out when they spotted Jill picking up trash. After a few days, she wondered, Would others like to walk with me?Excited, she posted on the Nextdoor app: 'I walk every morning and pick up trash. If you want to join, meet me in front of the coffee shop at 8 AM'. The next day, she was stunned to see a dozen people show up. She handed out bags and together, they cleaned up a nearby park.When they were all done, they went for a coffee. "When can we do this again?" everyone asked. Soon, every morning, Jill and a rotating crew gathered for two hours of walking and cleaning. She named her group Volunteers Cleaning Communities. They turned in recyclables found on streets, parks and a stretch of State Route 118 and used the cash to buy heavy-duty bags, vests and backpacks.After COVID restrictions lifted, more than 100 people began showing up at least once a week. To keep things interesting, Jill also organised a game night every third month and a monthly birthday celebration. VCC members have formed close friendships. One couple even met, fell in love and got married.“They are my new family,” says Emilie Koster, a former UCLA volunteer. “When COVID struck, we volunteers were the first to be sent home. Then I heard about VCC. It’s easier to do something meaningful when you’re with like-minded people.” Over the past six years, VCC members have removed and disposed of nearly three-quarters of a million pounds of trash. “And that doesn’t include the larger items we set out for the city,” Jill said to Woman's World. “We get exercise, improve the community and make friends. It’s a win all around.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: An 82-year-old California tea importer spent 53 years on a 2-acre compound with 36+ structures; after decades of permit disputes and a 2024 National Register listing, a court ordered him to leave
articles.summary: US News: For more than half a century, two acres in the hills of Lagunitas became the home, workplace and personal vision of California tea importer David Lee .
articles.body: For more than half a century, two acres in the hills of Lagunitas became the home, workplace and personal vision of California tea importer David Lee Hoffman. Over the decades, the property evolved into a maze of handmade buildings, caves and other structures, earning the name The Last Resort. Now, after years of legal battles over permits and code enforcement, Hoffman has been forced to leave, reports SFGATE. Scroll down to read his journey of struggle.A decades-long building battleAccording to SFGATE, Hoffman, 82, moved onto the Marin County property more than 53 years ago. Beginning in the 1970s and 1980s, he constructed structures that supported his approach to sustainable living and provided storage for his tea business and other belongings. The compound eventually grew to at least 36 structures, many of them built without the permits required by the county. A neighbor's tip brought the property to the county's attention. Officials issued the first stop-work order in 1988, beginning a long-running dispute over whether the structures should be removed, legalized or preserved.The report adds that the legal process continued for decades and in 2015, a court placed the property under receivership, but the case remained active as attorneys representing Hoffman sought additional time and the county granted extensions.Recognition complicates the pictureWhile the county pursued enforcement, the unusual compound developed a following among architects, neighbors, environmentalists and others fascinated by its unconventional design. As per SFGATE, Marin County's Architectural Commission recognized the property's architectural significance in 2016. A year later, a petition supporting Hoffman attracted 7,132 signatures. The property's historic status received an additional boost in 2024, when The Last Resort was added to the National Register of Historic Places. The designation, however, did not resolve the underlying dispute over its unpermitted construction.Hoffman has acknowledged that the buildings lacked proper permits but has maintained that they were not unsafe. Enforcement actions and fines did little to prevent continued activity at the property, adds the report.Ordered to leaveThe long-running case reached a decisive point when Marin County Superior Court ordered Hoffman to vacate the compound. A court-appointed receiver took control of the property on Sept. 15, according to the county. And now, it remains unclear when the property will be put up for sale. Hoffman is temporarily staying with friends as he considers what comes next. Friends helped remove the tea and some artwork from the compound, but much of his property remains behind. Hoffman estimated that as much as 50,000 pounds of tea had been stored inside the hand-built caves, informs the online report.An uncertain futureThe legal battle has also come at considerable personal cost. Hoffman estimates he has spent about $1 million on attorney fees over the years. His current attorney is continuing to represent him without payment. For now, the future of The Last Resort remains uncertain.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: How hotter and drier summers could change London’s parks
articles.summary: Kew and The Royal Parks are changing how they plant and water as drought puts pressure on green spaces.
articles.body:
London may have to change what it plants and how it looks after its green spaces as hotter and drier summers put increasing pressure on water supplies.

Thames Water, which supplies most of the capital, said water levels had not yet recovered from this year's record-breaking hot summer, with sustained rainfall needed before it could consider lifting hosepipe restrictions.

The conditions are prompting some of London's green spaces, including Kew Gardens and the Royal Parks, to rethink how they plan for the future.

Some trees could see their lifespans shortened by prolonged heat, while more drought-resistant plants could become a common sight across the capital.

July was the driest month on record in southern England, with Kew Gardens recording no measurable rainfall.

At Kew, work is under way to rethink planting and watering, including choosing species that require less water and using captured water for irrigation.

Among these drought-resilient plants is agave montana, a succulent from the mountains of Mexico which needs little watering and belongs to the same plant family as the crop used to make tequila.

"In the midst of a hosepipe ban, this is quite a good selection to make," said Thomas Freeth, head of collection management at Kew Gardens.

While hosepipes and sprinklers are restricted in parks and public gardens, Kew is exempt in order to protect its National Plant Collections.

Freeth said: "We just have to think more carefully about where the water comes from.

"We have installed a glorified water butt recently as a low-tech solution and that saw three of our most water-intensive glasshouses right through to the end of July."

The Royal Parks is also preparing for hotter, drier conditions, which could significantly shorten the lifespan of some of London's established trees.

Darren Share, director of parks at The Royal Parks, said: "Where we'd expect there to be another 150 odd years' left growth in them, they might only have between 50 and 70 years now, so it's half.

"It's something we need to continue to keep an eye on."

A recent report from the Greater London Authority found that, if nothing changes, over 72% of London's current public realm tree population will struggle under future climate conditions.

Trees can help make London more resilient to heat, providing the city with shade and protection from more extreme weather.

Thames Water said it would continue monitoring rainfall and water levels, with hosepipe restrictions kept under review.

A spokesperson said: "Changing weather patterns, a growing population and the need to reduce environmental impacts are all putting pressure on water resources.

"The South East is one of the UK's driest regions, classified by the Environment Agency as 'seriously water stressed'. If we do nothing, we face a shortfall of one billion litres a day by 2050."

The company said two-thirds of people it recently polled were worried about a consistent water supply, while fewer than a third believed supplies would always be plentiful.

It said new water sources, including the White Horse Reservoir and Teddington drought-resilience scheme, would be needed alongside efforts to cut leaks and water use.

articles.title: In 2014, a detectorist uncovered 5,248 Anglo-Saxon coins four days before Christmas; the £1.35m reward was shared with the landowner whose field held them
articles.summary: UK News: In December 2014, metal detectorist Paul Coleman uncovered a remarkable hoard of 5,248 Anglo-Saxon coins from King Cnut's reign, valued at £1.35 million, marking it as the largest find in 150 years.
articles.body: Metal detectorist Paul Coleman discovered a bundle of 5,248 silver pennies from King Cnut's reign in December 2014, shortly before Christmas, at Lenborough near Buckingham. This became the biggest coin treasure under the Treasure Act 1996 and was shared as a reward between Paul Coleman, who discovered it, and the landowner of Lenborough.Paul Coleman's find at a Lenborough rally, 21 December 2014In February 2015, Rory Naismith, a historian, wrote on the Anglo-Saxon, Norse & Celtic blog that the hoard had come to light on 21 December 2014, during a metal-detecting rally at Lenborough, Buckinghamshire. Gareth Williams's preliminary report in Anglo-Saxon England, published by Cambridge University Press, counts 5,248 silver pennies wrapped in a sheet of lead. Country Life later mentioned Coleman's discovery in a 22 November 2019 article by Carla Passino on treasure theft, which held up Lenborough as a find that was correctly handled. Art Fund's acquisition record calls it the largest Saxon coin hoard recorded in Britain in more than 150 years.The 5,248-penny count and two distinct parcels of coinsThe first detailed account is Gareth Williams's A hoard from the reign of Cnut from Buckinghamshire: a preliminary report, printed in volume 44 of Anglo-Saxon England, dated December 2015, a year after the find. The paper describes the find as one of the largest hoards of Anglo-Saxon coins ever discovered. It comprised 5,248 silver pennies, found at Lenborough in December 2014. Williams cannot date the burial precisely, but concludes it took place in the latter part of Cnut's reign, between 1016 and 1035. Since the entire group was enclosed by lead wrappers, the study by Williams states that it is one deposit. Within it, the coins are divided into several groups. One of them belongs to the period of King Æthelred II (978 to 1016), and the other one belongs to the time of King Cnut later in his reign (1016 to 1035).The significance of this finding comes from the fact that the make-up of the 5,248 silver pennies aids in identifying the exact time period during which the Lenborough hoard was buried. Williams adds that the hoard contains few coins of particular numismatic interest, with the Agnus Dei mule discussed below as one notable exception. Nevertheless, it can shed light on how late Anglo-Saxon coinage was administered during Cnut's reign.One Agnus Dei mule among almost 1,000 coins of Æthelred IISimon Keynes and Rory Naismith examined a single coin from the hoard in A new Agnus Dei/Last Small Cross mule, published in the same journal. A mule pairs a die from one coin type with a die from another. Keynes and Naismith report that the Lenborough hoard yielded the twenty-third coin struck from Agnus Dei dies and only the second known mule pairing an Agnus Dei obverse with a Last Small Cross reverse. The paper goes on further to point out the unique nature of the coin: only one coin of that type was found among nearly 1,000 coins of King Æthelred II.This coin is identified in their research as the twenty-third specimen made using the Agnus Dei dies. This is also the second Agnus Dei mule which bears a reverse design of the Last Small Cross. Before Lenborough, there had been only three finds of Agnus Dei pennies in England, thus making this find the first hoard to include such a specimen. Also, it should be noted that a single specimen of this coin among 985 coins of Æthelred II makes this issue very rare indeed. This is a coin that was struck in Leicester by Æthelwig the moneyer and weighed 1.46 grams, as stated in the Fitzwilliam Museum’s Early Medieval Corpus. It has the same dies as the only known coin of Æthelwig and adds up to four known coins of Leicester. It is shown in Figure 7 in Williams' study cited above.The £1.35 million valuation and the 50:50 reward ruleAny find that a museum wishes to acquire goes before the Treasure Valuation Committee. The committee's page on GOV.UK explains that it commissions a provisional valuation from experts in the antiquities or coin trades. The finders, the landowner and the museum have their say, after which the committee assesses the items to determine the value. The same GOV.UK page adds that rewards are usually split equally between the finder and the landowner unless other arrangements have been made. Moreover, the committee may decrease a reward in cases where the finder has been found guilty of committing an offence according to the law, or was illegally on the land. In the case of Lenborough, the records of the Art Fund show a total cost of £1,350,000, out of which £250,000 was granted by the charity itself. Country Life notes that Coleman and the landowner shared a reward based on the £1.35 million valuation.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 10-year-old Seattle boy lived in a tent while his mother battled fentanyl addiction; after an 11-month rescue effort, he entered school for the first time and said, 'I want to go back'
articles.summary: US News: A 10-year-old boy in Seattle walked into a school for the first time last week after spending much of his childhood living in a tent in a North Seattl.
articles.body: A 10-year-old boy in Seattle walked into a school for the first time last week after spending much of his childhood living in a tent in a North Seattle park. His first day of school came after an 11-month effort by a local nonprofit, neighbours and others to help him and his mother move out of life on the streets.The boy had been living in the tent with his mother, who was struggling with fentanyl addiction and was being sexually exploited, according to Kristine Moreland, executive director of The More We Love, a Kirkland-based organisation that works with homeless women and children, KRI reported. The boy's father had also refused offers of housing, food and other services.Moreland said the boy had been living in difficult conditions and had never experienced school before. “This young man has been in fight or flight since the day he was born,” she said. After his first day in the classroom, however, the boy gave the people who had been helping him a simple response. “I want to go back.”His journey towards school began in October last year, when Moreland and her team first visited the tent where the boy was living. At the time, he was alone in the tent. The situation had already drawn the attention of neighbours, who had repeatedly contacted the Seattle Police Department and Child Protective Services.Neighbours kept raising concernsAccording to Moreland, authorities had determined on several occasions that the boy was not in imminent danger. The nonprofit, however, continued visiting the tent and trying to help the family.“Everybody kept saying the same thing: He is ok. He is safe,” Moreland said. “We continued to show up at that tent, knowing that that was not the case.”The situation received wider attention in December after KIRO Newsradio reported on the boy. Moreland was recorded offering the family immediate shelter, including a private room that was available that day. The boy's father rejected the offer. “Not from you,” he told her.The situation changed in the early hours of New Year's Day. A Seattle police officer called Moreland and told her that the boy and his mother were ready to accept help. The mother entered treatment for active fentanyl addiction, while The More We Love helped connect her with recovery services.The organisation also arranged behavioural health treatment for the boy through Seattle Children's Hospital. Moreland said her team worked with another mission to find long-term housing for the family. However, that agency was unable to manage the boy's behavioural challenges and the family was released back to the streets.That did not end the effort to help them. “We said, not a chance. Our case managers have dug in day after day, helping this little man get through this,” Moreland said.A fresh new startThe boy's mother remains in recovery, Moreland said. She described that progress as a big deal while also pointing to the difficulties involved in learning to parent while dealing with addiction and trauma.“She has been in the cycle predominantly her whole life,” Moreland said. “We really have to work on her traumas as well.”For the boy, the nonprofit's work did not stop with getting him into school. Moreland said the boy still faces challenges as he adjusts to a new life, including the possibility of being bullied at school. She said people should not romanticise what comes next simply because he has now reached a classroom.“And what if he was still living in the tent?” Moreland said. “Then where would he be?”Many families still need helpMoreland said the boy's situation is not unique. She said she receives calls every day from law enforcement and community partners about women and children living in encampments across the region.The More We Love has also received a $500,000 matching donation from an anonymous donor to support efforts to help women and children living in encampments. Moreland said donations to the organisation through its website would be matched.The privately funded nonprofit also operates a crisis centre where staff care for infants born exposed to fentanyl. Moreland said the organisation needs volunteers to help comfort and care for the babies.Moreland has worked in outreach in Seattle for nearly 25 years. She said the 10-year-old now has “an army of encouragement behind him” as he begins school and adjusts to a different life. “This is hope to me,” she said. “And reminds me to continue every single day in this work.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
