articles.title: North Korea fires  ballistic missile amid rising regional tensions
articles.summary: International News: North Korea fired a short range ballistic missile toward the East Sea on Sunday, with the launch detected from the Wonsan area, South Korea’s military.
articles.body: North Korea fired a short range ballistic missile toward the East Sea on Sunday, with the launch detected from the Wonsan area, South Korea’s military said. The launch marks another weapons test by Pyongyang amid heightened military tensions on the Korean Peninsula.According to South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff, the missile was launched at around 3 pm local time and flew toward the East Sea. The military was continuing to analyse its exact specifications and flight details.The launch follows another round of missile activity by North Korea days earlier. On September 12, Pyongyang fired multiple short range ballistic missiles from the Wonsan area, with South Korea saying the weapons travelled about 250 km toward the East Sea.North Korea later described the September 12 launches as part of a firepower strike drill involving tactical ballistic and cruise missiles, large calibre multiple rocket launchers and attack drones, according to its state media.The September 12 launches came a day after South Korea, the US and Japan concluded their five day Freedom Edge military exercise. Pyongyang had criticised the drills, with North Korean Defence Minister Kim Song Gi warning that the country would take what he called “strong and reflective countermeasures” against military provocations.The latest launch also comes amid increasingly sharp rhetoric from Pyongyang over US led military activity in the region. Kim Yo Jong, the sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and a senior ruling party official, on September 18 accused Washington and its allies of worsening tensions on the Korean Peninsula and said North Korea would continue strengthening its nuclear deterrent.

articles.title: German elections under way which could decide fate of Chancellor Merz
articles.summary: The chancellor is facing intense political pressure which will increase if his party struggles in Sunday's polls.
articles.body:
Local elections are taking place in two German states on Sunday which could increase the political pressure on Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

Opinion polls in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Vorpommerm suggest Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) is at risk of damaging defeats, which would raise further questions about the chancellor's future.

These latest elections come after the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party won a major victory in the state of Saxony-Anhalt two weeks ago, while the CDU saw its vote halved.

There has been speculation in Germany that Merz could be replaced as chancellor mid-term unless the CDU's political fortunes improve.

He has said he will carry on but is facing poor approval ratings amid rumours of a so-called chancellor swap, though his challengers are "still hesitating", writes German news site Tagesschau .

According to the polls, Merz's conservatives could lose power in Berlin as it tussles with Die Linke (The Left) over first place.

Meanwhile in the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the CDU has only just been hovering above the 5% threshold needed for a party to enter the state parliament. It could spell their worst ever result in a state election.

How did it come to this after just 16 months in power? Friedrich Merz is having to answer for the tumbling popularity of his own party, while the political force that he aimed to counter - the AfD - continues its rise.

Some branches of the AfD are classed as right-wing extremist by domestic intelligence, a designation it strongly rejects.

But its anti-immigration, Russian-friendly, Germany-first agenda has found fertile ground in the country's former communist east.

The AfD is hoping to build on its recent landslide win in Saxony-Anhalt by topping the polls in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.

However, the centre-left SPD has staged a late comeback to be in contention for the top spot through its lead candidate, Manuela Schwesig.

Currently the state premier, Schwesig is trying to sweep up the anti-AfD vote as she bills herself as the "Die Frau gegen Blau" - "Woman against Blue", the AfD's party colours.

But her local popularity belies the far poorer fortunes of her national party which is locked in a loveless coalition with Merz's CDU.

In a queue for a campaign event in the city of Neubrandenburg, AfD supporter Reinhart tells us that the traditional parties are being washed away.

"Not only in Germany. In Italy, in France, in Great Britain. Everywhere the traditional parties go down."

He smiles when asked what he thinks of Merz, saying: "Oh well everyone thinks the same about him.

"He is arrogant, out of touch, not on the same level as the general public."

Merz's backers argue that the chancellor has had a tough time with global events and that a lot of the problems the nation faces are ones he has inherited.

But whatever faith people had in his ability to fix those problems, it is apparently ebbing away - and, the brutal truth is, it can be hard to find voters who like him.

The former corporate lawyer's tack to the right on issues like immigration has failed to erode AfD support while also alienating people further to the left.

His blunt communication style has also caused irritation, such as his dismissal of "work-life balance", telling Germans they need to work more and take less sick leave.

Supporters would argue he is a man who is ready to administer the medicine the nation needs, even if people do not like the taste of it.

But the country's long-stuttering economy, high energy costs and fraught debates about immigration are feeding a sense of national gloom.

Earlier this week, the leaders of eight German states backed Merz and said restoring trust in the CDU lay in "listening ​and taking political action, not in debates ​over personnel".

But while no one within his party has openly challenged Merz for the top job, murmurings of discontent have grown louder.

Martin Rohloff, the CDU candidate for Neubrandenburg, thinks Merz does not have the "Fingerspitzengefühl, the feeling for the small persons".

"Maybe he wants the right things," muses Rohloff, but "he cannot communicate well".

Asked if Merz should go, he says it is not an easy question but: "If I have to answer yes or no, I would say yes. There are other people who maybe have better feelings for the public."

Merz has vowed to carry on as his coalition government aims to push through a package of economic, tax and welfare reforms that are finally due before parliament this autumn.

But Sunday's vote brings a danger for the chancellor - that he is already out of time.

The chancellor is reportedly due to meet senior party figures in Berlin on Sunday evening having already cancelled a planned trip next week to New York, in an apparent effort to contain the crisis.

A staunch backer of Ukraine, the fall of Friedrich Merz would trigger further instability in a continent already rocked by warnings of increased Russian aggression.

articles.title: In 1967, Rolex made a rare yellow-gold Daytona with a Paul Newman dial; after more than 45 years in a family drawer, two sisters inherited it and it sold for CHF 1.143 million in Geneva
articles.summary: Rest of World News: A rare Rolex Daytona made in 1967 and kept in a family drawer for more than 45 years sold for CHF 1.143 million at auction in Geneva. The 18k yellow-g.
articles.body: A rare Rolex Daytona made in 1967 and kept in a family drawer for more than 45 years sold for CHF 1.143 million at auction in Geneva. The 18k yellow-gold watch, a Reference 6239 with a black and champagne “Paul Newman” dial, belonged to the family of its original owner. It was later inherited by two sisters before being offered at auction.According to Phillips Auction, the watch was listed by Sotheby’s with an estimate of CHF 300,000 to CHF 600,000. Its final price was much higher than the auction house’s estimate. The sale drew attention to the rarity of yellow-gold versions of the early Rolex Daytona, particularly those fitted with the Paul Newman-style dial.The Reference 6239 has an important place in the history of the Daytona. Rolex launched the model in 1963, and it was discontinued only a few years later. Sotheby’s estimates that around 14,000 examples of the Reference 6239 were produced, with only about 300 made in yellow gold.That already makes the yellow-gold version a small part of the total production. The watch sold in Geneva is rarer still because of its Paul Newman dial. Sotheby’s research suggests that only about 10 gold Reference 6239 watches with Paul Newman dials have resurfaced on the market.A rare yellow-gold DaytonaThe watch has an 18k yellow-gold case measuring 37 mm in diameter. It has a black dial with champagne-coloured registers and is powered by Rolex calibre 722-1, a manually wound movement with 17 jewels. The case, dial and movement are all signed.Its case number is 1’757’928. The watch has a gold-plated Rolex buckle and a screw-down case back. It does not come with its original box, papers or other accessories.Sotheby’s said the watch came directly from the family of the original owner. It had been left forgotten in a drawer for more than 45 years. That history was an important part of the watch’s provenance when it was presented for sale. The watch was also described as being in exceptional condition.Why the Reference 6239 is importantThe Reference 6239 was the first Daytona model produced by Rolex, according to Sotheby’s. The model was launched in 1963 and was created for the world of endurance racing. Its design combined a mechanical chronograph with a tachymeter scale, features associated with its racing purpose.The few yellow-gold examples have details that set them apart from the more common steel watches. Sotheby’s described the gold versions as having refined dial details, champagne tones, gilt markers and distinctive graphics.The Paul Newman dial is another feature that makes these watches particularly sought after by collectors. The term refers to a specific dial layout used on some vintage Daytona models. The yellow-gold watch sold by Sotheby’s has a black dial with champagne registers.Another yellow-gold Reference 6239, known as “The Golden Pagoda”, was also highlighted by Phillips in its coverage of a 2025 Geneva auction. Phillips described that watch as having a champagne “Paul Newman” dial and said it was one of the rarest versions of the Daytona.Only about 300 yellow-gold examplesPhillips said that around 14,000 Reference 6239 Daytonas were produced between 1963 and 1969, while only about 300 were made in yellow gold. This means the gold version was a very small part of the total production.The yellow-gold watches also differed from the steel versions in their appearance. Phillips described the champagne Paul Newman dial as having a warm finish, with three recessed registers and gold graphics.The auction house also noted that gold was not the usual choice for a Daytona at the time. The Cosmograph was designed as a functional chronograph, while Rolex’s gold watches were more commonly associated with dressier models.Over time, however, rare examples of the Daytona became important pieces for collectors. articles.title: The University of Washington built an 86.4 kW solar canopy over part of a Husky Stadium parking lot; a larger future buildout could reach up to 8 MW
articles.summary: US News: When it comes to adding solar power on campus, universities often focus on rooftops, but the University of Washington saw promise in its parking lots .
articles.body: When it comes to adding solar power on campus, universities often focus on rooftops, but the University of Washington saw promise in its parking lots as well. The university has constructed a solar canopy over Lot E18, a length of asphalt north of Husky Stadium, that converts hundreds of parking spots into a source of renewable electricity without taking any spots out of use.The canopy, finished in February 2026 as a pilot project between UW Transportation Services and student-led group UW Solar, produces 86.4 kW that currently feeds directly into the university's electrical grid. The installation also adds 20 new electric-vehicle charging slots, giving students, staff and visitors a place to plug in while their cars rest under the panels during the day.Pairing solar canopies with EV charging in the same footprint means the same parking spot that shelters a car from rain or sun can also help power that car's next drive, at least in theory once battery storage or smarter routing of the canopy's output is added. For now, the 86.4 kW the canopy generates feeds directly into the university's electrical grid rather than to the chargers specifically, but the pairing signals how UW is thinking about parking lots as multi-purpose infrastructure rather than single-use space.Transforming a former landfill into an energy assetThe site was not chosen by accident. Lot E18 sits on land that was once Union Bay, then a city landfill, then a parking lot, and the university saw a chance to put a site with a complicated environmental history to better use. Union Bay's shift from wetland to landfill to parking lot reflects a pattern common across many American cities, where low-lying land near a body of water was filled in over decades of urban expansion and only much later reconsidered for restoration or reuse. Turning part of that legacy into a renewable energy source adds a new chapter to a site that has already changed use several times over the past century. The canopy sits above the existing rows of cars rather than replacing them, so no parking capacity is lost.Before construction, the university filed environmental documents outlining the scope of the work. Its public notice described plans for a roughly 4,820-square-foot canopy above 30 parking spaces, designed to connect eventually to both the City of Seattle's grid and the university's own, a dual link intended to let the system feed power in more than one direction once fully built out.A pilot with space for growthWhat's compelling about the E18 canopy isn't what it is now, but what it could become. Planners see potential for canopies across the entire E18 lot and the adjacent E01 lot, which together could generate up to 8 MW, enough to cover about 5 per cent of the university's total electricity demand. That 5 per cent figure might sound modest on its own, but for a campus of UW's size, even a single-digit share of total demand met through on-site solar represents a meaningful dent in the electricity the university would otherwise have to buy from off-campus sources. At a ribbon-cutting for the project, UW Solar's academic adviser and student leaders called the installation a template for what the rest of campus could one day follow.Much of the campus still relies on natural gas for heating and cooling steam, and cutting that reliance is central to the university's long-term sustainability strategy. The E18 canopy is part of a broader 2050 Sustainability Action Plan that treats parking lots as an underused resource rather than dead space. If the larger expansion goes ahead, a lot best known for tailgating before football games could end up as one of the more significant sources of renewable power on campus.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: AI helping speed up Worcestershire bus pass applications says council
articles.summary: Worcestershire County Council says the Bus Pass AI Agent has helped to process 2,500 applications.
articles.body:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is being used to help speed up bus pass applications in Worcestershire.

The Bus Pass AI Agent has helped process 2,500 applications and checked 7,500 uploaded documents at Worcestershire County Council in eight months.

The council said using the technology has helped free up staff time to focus on supporting residents while human oversight does remain in place.

It said the system found hundreds of issues that could have delayed applications and helped residents correct them earlier, reducing the need for repeated contact.

The technology helps identify common issues, such as incorrect photographs, proof of address documents or dates of birth, before an application reaches a member of staff for review. Staff continue to make the final decisions.

Deputy Leader, Councillor Adam Kent, said AI is helping the council make its services more efficient, reduce unnecessary administration and allow staff to spend more time focusing on the people who need support.

He said: "We will be accelerating our use of to improve the experience for residents, speed up processes and deliver better value for taxpayers.

"We're focused on using AI where it can solve real challenges and make a practical difference, helping us modernise services while maintaining the high standards residents rightly expect."

The council said its approach is to introduce AI within services where it can deliver clear benefits as part of its wider digital programme.

articles.title: In 1970, two Minnesota brothers set off to walk around Earth with a mule; after one was shot dead by bandits in Afghanistan, the survivor returned four years later to complete the journey
articles.summary: US News: In 1970, two Minnesota brothers embarked on a remarkable journey to walk around the globe with a mule. After tragedy struck with the death of one brother in Afghanistan, the survivor completed the journey alone, becoming the first to circumnavigate the Earth on foot, chronicled in this astonishing tale of adventure and resilience.
articles.body: On June 20, 1970, two brothers from Minnesota walked out of Waseca with an extraordinary plan: to circle the Earth on foot. David Kunst, 30, and his younger brother John, 22, set out with maps, a small amount of money and a mule named Willie Makeit, carrying their supplies. More than four years later, David returned to his hometown after completing what Guinness World Records recognised as the first independently verified circumnavigation of the globe on foot.According to Smithsonian Magazine, the journey covered about 14,450 miles across four continents and 13 countries. It began with the brothers walking from Minnesota to New York, after which they crossed the Atlantic by plane to Portugal and continued eastwards on foot. Their route took them through Europe, Turkey, Iran and Afghanistan before the expedition was transformed by a violent encounter in the Afghan mountains.From Minnesota to the edge of AsiaThe idea had grown from a conversation David had with a friend in Waseca. Looking for a new direction, he persuaded John to join him. Their departure became a local spectacle, with thousands of people gathering to watch the brothers leave town. Willie Makeit, the mule carrying their camping equipment, became part of the travelling team.The brothers relied heavily on the kindness of strangers as they travelled through unfamiliar countries. They also received much media coverage during their travels. This Journey also gave them an opportunity to meet Princess Grace of Monaco and Norwegian explorer Thor Heyerdahl; however, it was not always easy. They planned to traverse the Soviet Union, but they were denied permission. In August 1972, when the brothers reached Afghanistan, they were halfway into their journey.According to David Kunst, the Afghan landscape presented extreme heat, long stretches without water and concerns about banditry. The brothers had also become the subject of a damaging misunderstanding. An Afghan newspaper reportedly said they were collecting money for UNICEF rather than asking people to donate to the organisation. This error made it seem that the travellers were carrying a large amount of money.A night that ended one brother's journeyOn October 21, 1972, David and John were walking near a secluded road when armed men approached them. David said in retrospect that he believed the attackers thought that the two brothers had money on them. A shot hit David in the chest. John was shot to death. Seriously injured and fearing the attackers might shoot again, David pretended to be dead while they searched their belongings. He was later picked up by soldiers and taken to Kabul, where medical reports showed that the bullet had hit his left lung.John's death marked the end of the initial mission in tragedy. David returned to Minnesota to recuperate, yet the hike was far from over. Four months later, he decided to continue what he and John had begun. In March 1973, David returned to Afghanistan with another brother, Peter. The two continued walking towards Pakistan and India. David then walked from New Delhi to Calcutta on foot in 44 days.Four years, 21 pairs of shoes and a finishPolitical barriers also influenced the route choice. Unable to travel through the Soviet Union or China, David and Peter flew from India to Australia. Later, Peter had to leave the expedition, while David crossed Australia alone. David's supply cart became difficult to manage in Australia, and he had to drag it alone. Help arrived when Australian schoolteacher Jenni Samuel met him and used her car to help pull his cart.As per Guinness World Records, David Kunst completed his journey on October 5, 1974, after walking 23,250 kilometres (14,450 miles) across four continents. His own account records that the four-year, three-month and 16-day journey cost him 21 pairs of shoes. Guinness World Records recognises Kunst's achievement as the first verified circumnavigation of the world on foot. What began as a brothers' adventure ended as a solo achievement shaped by tragedy, politics, fatigue and acts of goodwill. While John did not return to his homeland, David managed to finish what they both started, thereby making one of the strangest walks of the 20th century known in writing.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: He scored just 52% in Class 10, failed IIT entrance exam 3 times and missed IIM: How Rahul Sinha went on to become an SDM in Bihar at 34
articles.summary: In 1999, Rahul Sinha scored 52% in Class 10. He then appeared for the IIT entrance examination three times and failed to qualify on every attempt. An .
articles.body: In 1999, Rahul Sinha scored 52% in Class 10. He then appeared for the IIT entrance examination three times and failed to qualify on every attempt. An attempt at the IIM entrance examination also did not work out. He eventually took up an ordinary job, got married and started a family. Yet, two decades after his Class 10 result, Sinha had a very different result to celebrate.On February 2, 2019, he was selected as a Sub-Divisional Magistrate (SDM) through the Bihar Public Service Commission (BPSC). He was 34 when he began preparing for the examination, while managing a job and family responsibilities. Today, Sinha works as an SDM in Sheikhpura district of Bihar. He also creates videos for aspirants on his YouTube channel, @Rahul Sinha, and has more than 2 million followers on Instagram.His story, which he has shared through his social media videos, is spread across nearly 20 years of academic setbacks and career uncertainty.“In my 10th grade, I scored only 52% marks”Sinha has often spoken about the academic setbacks that shaped his early years. In an Instagram video shared last year, he said, “In my 10th grade, I scored only 52% marks. After that, I gave 3 attempts in IIT. In all 3 attempts, I did not qualify for IIT.” The IIT attempts were not his only unsuccessful examinations. After completing his BTech, Sinha also prepared for the IIM entrance examination but could not clear it.Looking back, he said the failures continued to affect how he viewed himself. “I feel that people from Bihar often do not recognise their own potential. I made the same mistake. For almost 10 years, I believed that a government job was not something an ordinary person could achieve. I thought that some people were specially born to clear such exams,” he said in a video on his YouTube channel @Rahul Sinha.A school entrance exam changed how he saw himselfSinha said one of the early incidents that affected his confidence came after his father's transfer. He appeared for a school entrance examination but could not qualify. “I could not qualify for it. That affected my confidence, and that feeling continued for a long time,” he recalled in the video. He later completed his BTech from a private college. He still wanted to do something different, but did not know exactly what path to take. “At that time, many students were preparing for an MBA, so I thought I should prepare for it too. I started preparing for the IIM entrance exam, but I could not clear it,” he said.He then started working in an ordinary job. “But somewhere inside, the hurt from my childhood was still there. I wanted to prove myself,” he said.“I had been given the label of being below average"Sinha said that when results did not come, the pressure was not limited to the examinations themselves. Comments from relatives and society also became difficult to handle. He also recalled how his parents faced criticism when his attempts did not succeed. “When results were not coming, one of the most difficult things was dealing with the comments from relatives and society. Sometimes, your family has to face even more of those comments than you do. Your parents have to go through it,” he said.His father sent him to Kota for IIT preparationWhen Sinha was preparing for IIT, Kota had only recently begun emerging as a major coaching destination, according to him. He said his father decided to send him there. But Sinha did not qualify for IIT despite three attempts. He recalled that the failure also brought criticism for his parents. “When I could not clear the exam, people started saying, ‘Instead of doing this, you should have prepared him differently.’ My parents were also criticised for those decisions,” he said.At 34, he decided to try for BPSCSinha eventually got married in an arranged marriage and began living what he described as a normal life. He was working in Bangalore, earning a living and managing family responsibilities. But the desire to achieve something different remained. “I always felt that I had to do something. The only problem was that I did not know how,” he said.His first target became a government job. By then, he was 34. He said he realised that many examinations had an upper age limit of 32 for general-category candidates. He then came across BPSC. “Through BPSC, you can become an SDM or Deputy Collector, and the age limit was 37,” he said. That gave him a window to make another attempt.But this time, his circumstances were very different from those of a typical full-time aspirant. “At that time, I did not even know the syllabus properly. I was living in Bangalore and had a family to take care of. I was not a single bachelor who could leave everything and focus only on preparation. I had a family, and my baby was also about to be born. I had responsibilities,” he said.“It was an ‘if not now, then never’ situation for me,” he said.He studied at night and revised at workSinha began by looking for guidance on YouTube and studying whenever he found time. “At the job I was doing, I had access to a computer. I used to read something on the computer whenever I got time. Then I was transferred to a place where I did not have computer access,” he said. Instead of stopping his preparation, he changed his study method. “Whatever I studied at night, I would revise during the day at my office,” he said. He connected this approach with a line by Bhagat Singh that he had once read: “You can tie my body, but you cannot tie my mind.” “I applied that idea to my life. I studied at night and recalled what I had studied throughout the day,” he said.“Okay, I can do this”The preparation eventually proved fruitful. He cleared the preliminary examination. Clearing the prelims gave Sinha the confidence that had been missing for years. “Then I qualified for the preliminary exam. That gave me happiness and motivation. I thought, ‘Okay, I can do this,’” he said. The next challenge was the mains examination, where answer writing played an important role. “I decided that I would write as many answers as possible. Sometimes I wrote answers for eight or nine hours a day,” he said.He cleared the mains. Then came the interview. “After that, I cleared the interview,” he said. But even as he moved closer to his goal, his financial situation was difficult. “The day my final result came, I had only a very small amount of money left in my bank account,” he recalled.February 2, 2019: The result dayOn February 2, 2019, Sinha finally got the result he had been waiting for. “I got the SDM post for which I had worked so hard,” he said. The moment was particularly emotional because of how far he had travelled from his school years. “That was the first time I cried. In 1999, I had scored 52 per cent in Class 10. In 2019, I was selected as an SDM,” he said. “It was almost a 20-year journey. In those 20 years, I faced many failures and setbacks, but I did not cry. That day, I cried for the first time,” he said.“My wife supported me greatly”Sinha also spoke about the role his wife played during the period when he was preparing for BPSC while managing financial and family responsibilities. “Throughout this journey, my wife supported me greatly. When you are financially weak, the support of your wife becomes very important,” he said.In one of his Instagram videos, he summed up the message he wants aspirants to take from his own experience: “What is your previous record? What is not there in your life? What is there? It does not matter. Whenever you wake up, you will win.”Looking for trusted parenting advice? articles.title: Harrogate MP calls for Yorkshire to get its own parliament
articles.summary: Harrogate Lib Dem MP Tom Gordon says Yorkshire devolution should go further than elected mayors.
articles.body:
A Liberal Democrat MP has called on Prime Minister Andy Burnham to go further with his devolution plans and give Yorkshire its own parliament.

Harrogate and Knaresborough MP Tom Gordon said too much power was currently in the hands of elected mayors and a Yorkshire parliament would better reflect the region.

Burnham has recently set out plans to give elected mayors more power over planning and tackling fly-tipping and said he would give them a share of income tax and business rates.

But Gordon told BBC Politics North he believed that giving more money and powers to four separate Yorkshire mayoralties actually deepened divides in the county and a Yorkshire parliament would be "a good thing".

Yorkshire currently has three Labour mayors - Oliver Coppard for South Yorkshire, Tracy Brabin for West Yorkshire and David Skaith for York and North Yorkshire - as well as Luke Campbell, the Reform UK mayor of Hull and East Yorkshire.

Gordon said Yorkshire had a population larger than Scotland and an economy larger than Wales, and, as such, it should have a parliament with a broader spectrum of views represented, rather than so much power resting with the four elected mayors.

The Lib Dem said that while people had been told the recent local government reorganisation in North Yorkshire would "simplify" the situation, he believed that was not the case.

"We've ended up with a new North Yorkshire Council at a higher tier and a Harrogate town council below it, so we've ended up with two tiers. In fact, there's a third tier when you throw in the regional mayor," he said.

"So we've ended up with more tiers, but those powers have been moved upwards rather than down to people.

"I think we owe it to have everyone have a seat at that table, not just all that power put in one person's hands."

Gordon said he believed a Yorkshire parliament was the way forward "if it's good enough for Scotland, if it's good enough for Wales, if it's good enough for London".

"We should have a model where we have broader people elected to it who can feed in all those issues into a Yorkshire-wide parliament. That, to me, is only a good thing," he said.

The idea of a Yorkshire parliament has previously been advocated by the Yorkshire Party.

Since 2014, the party has argued that it would create a more "engaged, democratic society".

Meanwhile, when devolution deals were first being discussed, a proposal was put forward for one mayor for all of Yorkshire.

The so-called "One Yorkshire" plan was backed by 18 of the region's 20 local councils, while Sheffield and Rotherham opted for a separate South Yorkshire solution.

However, the then Conservative Communities Secretary James Brokenshire rejected the proposal and said the plan did "not meet our criteria" .

Deals were later done for the four counties within Yorkshire

In a speech earlier this year, Burnham said decision-making needed to be "pushed to regions and local communities" , adding that it would see "good growth in every postcode".

Responding to Gordon's comments, Skaith said the Greater Manchester and Liverpool City Region, which has had devolved powers for longer, had worked "really well".

But Skaith also said he believed that all views were represented within the current system.

"It's not just four mayors who sit in Yorkshire, all our combined authorities are made up of those local authorities as well," he said.

"So, I'm not making decisions sat in York and North Yorkshire on my own. It's in partnership with the two local authorities."

Skaith pointed to the so-called "White Rose Agreement", signed by himself and the mayors of South and West Yorkshire, pledging to work closer on things like transport.

“Rail is a classic case - Northern Powerhouse Rail - where we got particularly the working around York station and the wider area of North Yorkshire," he said.

"We have got that collective buy-in as to what we want for Yorkshire for rail.

"That's why we've got so far with government, because we work collectively as mayors, because we know our transport is so interconnected."

When he was prime minister, David Cameron, together with Chancellor George Osborne, previously introduced "devolution deals".

Successive Conservative governments have extended those deals and powers for regional mayors.

However, York Conservative councillor Chris Steward warned that a parliament for Yorkshire would be "an absurd, costly and bureaucratic nonsense".

"I am a proud Yorkshireman, having lived here all my life," he said.

"But while it is a county for so much - from the scenery to county cricket to all the things making it famous - as we saw in the discussions about devolution, it is not a functional economic geography and politics viewed across the region would not work.

"People do not want yet another layer of politicians and the related expenses."

Reform UK has been approached for comment.

articles.title: In 1962, a German toolmaker rode away on a bicycle with almost no money; 52 years and about 403,000 miles later, he had pedalled through 196 countries
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In November 1962, Heinz Stücke left his hometown of Hövelhof in Westphalia on a three-speed bicycle with no fixed return date. He was 22, had trained .
articles.body: In November 1962, Heinz Stücke left his hometown of Hövelhof in Westphalia on a three-speed bicycle with no fixed return date. He was 22, had trained as a toolmaker and had grown increasingly reluctant to spend his life working in a factory. What began as an attempt to see the world became one of the longest bicycle journeys ever undertaken. Over the decades that followed, Stücke travelled hundreds of thousands of kilometres, crossed continents and eventually visited 196 countries.According to CYCLINGABOUT, accounts published around 2010 put Heinz Stücke's total distance at more than 609,000 kilometres, or about 378,000 miles. Later records put the eventual distance at around 648,000 kilometres. The 2010 figure reflects only part of his journey, since Stücke continued travelling for several more years before returning to Germany.A journey that was never meant to last decadesAs per Der Spiegel, Stücke did not initially leave Germany intending to spend decades travelling. His first major plan was to cycle towards Japan for the 1964 Olympic Games, but the journey soon developed beyond its original purpose. He eventually reached Japan in 1971, years later than planned, after choosing to continue exploring rather than hurry towards a fixed destination.Money was a constant problem. Stücke did not have many funds, and therefore devised his own system of financing his lifestyle. He would sell postcards, brochures, and pictures he took when travelling. Later, photography became central to his travels, and he amassed more than 100,000 pictures of the people and places he visited. The bicycle was as remarkable as the journey itself. Stücke spent almost the whole time during the expedition cycling on a steel-framed three-speed touring bicycle. The bike was heavily loaded and constantly repaired, remaining an item of equipment for decades of travelling. The bicycle was reportedly stolen several times but was always recovered.From seeing the world to seeing every countryDuring the first twenty years, the trips of Stücke were motivated mainly by curiosity and not by his goal to create an official world tour list. That desire emerged in the early 1980s, when Stücke decided he wanted to see every country in the world. The criteria changed as borders shifted and new countries emerged. Stücke believed that by 1996 he had completed his task and visited the Seychelles. Nevertheless, completing the list did not bring him the pleasure he expected, because he felt he had not spent enough time in some countries.He also faced dangers well beyond ordinary cyclist fatigue, including being knocked off his bike by a truck in the Atacama Desert and being chased through the streets of Haiti by an angry mob. Political boundaries and the international situation at that time also dictated how and where he could go.According to ABC News, Heinz Stücke was recognised by Guinness World Records in the 1990s for having travelled more widely by bicycle than anyone else. Stücke continued travelling, visiting more countries and documenting his experiences through photographs, gradually turning what began as a youthful adventure into a way of life that lasted for decades.196 countries and a lifetime on two wheelsWhen he finally came back home after all those travels, the numbers had swelled far past what his initial vision had been. His final tally was estimated at 648,000 kilometres, or 403,000 miles, and he visited 196 countries as well as many others. He used 21 passports and created extensive photographic and written records of his travels. His case is notable not for record-breaking round-the-world travel, but because the idea of a destination eventually became irrelevant to him. articles.title: A Florida woman spent 18 months turning a simple idea into a permanent Rainbow Bridge pet memorial; the community-built space in Fort Myers is now opening for families to leave collars and tags
articles.summary: US News: Florida resident Gabrielle Bolen has opened a permanent Rainbow Bridge Pet Memorial at the Alliance for the Arts in Fort Myers, giving families a plac.
articles.body: Florida resident Gabrielle Bolen has opened a permanent Rainbow Bridge Pet Memorial at the Alliance for the Arts in Fort Myers, giving families a place to remember pets they have lost, Cape Coral Breeze reported.The memorial opened on Saturday after Bolen spent about 18 months planning, fundraising and working with local businesses and community members to turn her idea into a physical space where visitors can leave collars and tags in honour of their pets.Bolen, a lifelong dog lover, had been working on the project for more than a year before it became a reality. The memorial was created as a place for people to grieve, remember and celebrate pets that were part of their families. The memorial is inspired by the well-known Rainbow Bridge poem.A place to remember lost petsThe Rainbow Bridge Pet Memorial is designed as a symbolic bridge that visitors can walk around rather than across. The structure is surrounded by landscaping and a seating area, creating a space where people can spend time remembering their pets.Visitors are invited to bring a collar or tag belonging to a pet they have lost. These tributes will become part of the memorial and create an evolving display of the bonds between people and their animals.“What started as a simple idea grew into something much larger than I ever imagined,” Bolen said in a prepared statement. “This bridge truly was built by a community of people who understand how deeply our pets become part of our families.”Bolen said the completed memorial was emotional for her after the long process of bringing the project together.“Seeing it completed is incredibly emotional, and I hope this space becomes a place where people can come to remember, to grieve, to celebrate and to feel connected to others who understand that kind of love,” she said.Local community helped build the memorialBolen spent more than a year working on planning, making connections and fundraising for the project. After the groundbreaking ceremony in August, local businesses and community members helped turn the plan into a completed memorial.Support for the project included funding, construction, labour, materials, engineering, signage, landscaping and other services.Every donor, including businesses, service providers and individual contributors, will be recognised with a commemorative plaque near the memorial.Bolen said the community support helped make the memorial something larger than the original idea. “This bridge truly was built by a community of people who understand how deeply our pets become part of our families,” she said.Memorial becomes permanent part of ArtsParkThe Rainbow Bridge Pet Memorial is now a permanent part of the Alliance for the Arts campus. The Alliance sees the project as part of its wider ArtsPark initiative, which aims to create arts, nature and community experiences across its 10-acre campus.Neil Volz, executive director of the Alliance for the Arts, said the memorial would add another space where people can connect with art and nature.“The Rainbow Bridge Pet Memorial is creating a place where residents and visitors can experience the arts alongside nature as a source of healing, connection, and enjoyment right in the heart of Fort Myers,” Volz said. “The Alliance is honoured to be the home of this special space.”The Alliance for the Arts is located at 10091 McGregor Blvd. in Fort Myers. The nonprofit visual and performing arts centre has been working in the community since 1975.“I think this space will mean something different to everyone who visits,” Bolen said. “For some, it may be a place to remember a pet they’ve recently lost. For others, it may bring back memories of an animal who was part of their family many years ago.”“My hope is that children and adults alike can find comfort here and know that they aren’t alone in their grief. The love we have for our pets is real, and that love deserves a place to be remembered,” she said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Afghan man arrested over suspected synagogue arson attempt in Germany ahead of holiest Jewish day
articles.summary: Europe News: A 37-year-old Afghan man was arrested in Germany on Thursday on suspicion of trying to set fire to a synagogue in Wuppertal, western Germany, just day.
articles.body: A 37-year-old Afghan man was arrested in Germany on Thursday on suspicion of trying to set fire to a synagogue in Wuppertal, western Germany, just days before Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar.According to German media reports, the suspect allegedly threw bags containing flammable liquid at the Bergische Synagogue, poured more of the liquid near a side entrance and set it ablaze.Members of the Jewish community managed to extinguish the flames within minutes, preventing the fire from spreading. No injuries were reported.Suspect allegedly made antisemitic remarksGerman prosecutors said the man allegedly made antisemitic remarks at the scene, according to the German Press Agency (DPA). Police said preliminary investigations indicated that he acted alone.The suspect fled after setting the liquid on fire but was later arrested. He has a previous conviction for threatening a neighbour, DPA reported.Wuppertal Mayor Johannes Slawig condemned the incident as “utterly despicable” and called for solidarity with the city's Jewish community.The Central Council of Jews in Germany also condemned the suspected attack, with its president Josef Schuster describing it as evidence of what he called the “progressive normalization of hatred towards Jews” in Germany.Synagogue had been targeted in 2014The European Jewish Congress said the timing of the incident was particularly disturbing as Jewish communities prepare for Yom Kippur. It called for Jews to be able to practise their faith and observe the High Holidays safely.US Special Envoy to Monitor and Combat Antisemitism Rabbi Yehuda Kaploun thanked local authorities for swiftly arresting the suspect, saying the attack would not succeed in spreading fear among Jews.The Bergische Synagogue was previously targeted in 2014, when three Palestinians were convicted after admitting to throwing incendiary objects at the building, according to DPA.The latest incident comes as Germany continues to deal with concerns over antisemitic attacks and crimes.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘Taking him back with us’: Nigel Farage wants to 'hijack' Trump’s ICE adviser to secure UK borders
articles.summary: UK News: Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has said he wants to “hijack” US President Donald Trump’s immigration adviser Tom Homan and bring him to Britain to help.
articles.body: Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has said he wants to “hijack” US President Donald Trump’s immigration adviser Tom Homan and bring him to Britain to help “secure our borders”.Speaking at an event in the US where Homan was a guest, Farage said: “I’ve got terrible news for you. We’re hijacking Tom Homan and taking him back with us to secure our borders.”Farage praises Trump administrationAccording to The Guardian, Farage also urged Europe to take a “more sensible view” of the Trump administration rather than portraying it as “villainous” through traditional mainstream media.Homan is a key Trump adviser on US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), which has faced scrutiny over its immigration enforcement tactics, including fatal shootings involving its agents. Farage has previously praised Homan’s approach to deportations, describing him as uncompromising.Reform UK has backed a strict immigration policy, including mass deportations of people who entered the UK illegally and using the Royal Navy to intercept migrant boats crossing the English Channel.Farage's changing stance on TrumpFarage has earlier appeared to distance himself from Trump, saying in April that the two had not spoken for several months and questioning the US president’s judgment over the Iran war.However, during his latest US trip, Farage defended Trump’s administration and said European countries should have a more balanced view of the US president.Farage has also differed with Trump on Northern Ireland. After Trump said earlier this week that he would like to see a united Ireland, Farage said Northern Ireland was a “proud and integral part” of the United Kingdom and that people there did not want a referendum or unification.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Smriti Mandhana creates history in Asain Games semi-final, becomes leading run-scorer in Women's T20I
articles.summary: Smriti Mandhana became the highest run-scorer in women’s T20I cricket, surpassing Suzie Bates, and the first Indian woman to hit 100 sixes in the format duri...
articles.body:
Smriti Mandhana made history in the Asian Games 2026 semi-final, becoming the highest run-scorer in women's T20I cricket. The India opener achieved the milestones during a blistering start against Bangladesh, as India raced to 71/1 in the powerplay in their bid to book a place in the gold-medal match. India captain Harmanpreet Kaur won the toss and elected to bat first in the second semi-final. Mandhana and Shafali Verma provided an explosive start, putting Bangladesh's bowlers under pressure from the outset.

Mandhana struck 37 off just 19 deliveries, hitting five fours and two sixes before her innings ended in the final over of the powerplay. She attempted another slog sweep off Nahida Akter but mistimed the shot, with Sobhana Mostary completing the catch at deep mid-wicket. Despite her dismissal, Mandhana had already etched her name in the record books, moving past New Zealand's Suzie Bates to become the leading run-scorer in women's T20Is. She also became the first Indian woman to reach 100 sixes in the format.

Shafali joined Mandhana in attacking Bangladesh's bowling, helping India reach 71/1 in the first six overs. The opening stand gave India early momentum in a high-stakes contest, with a place in the gold-medal match on the line.

articles.title: Artists turn Guernsey greenhouses into unexpected galleries
articles.summary: The exhibitions allow visitors to meet growers and learn about the island's agricultural industry.
articles.body:
A group of local artists are transforming working greenhouses into temporary art galleries as part of a project celebrating the island's growing heritage and encouraging people to reconnect with food production.

The exhibition, organised by the Guernsey Art Network, is taking place across three greenhouses over three September weekends.

Following a successful opening event at Bailiwick Blue in Vazon, the exhibition moves to Cornucopia at Belmont Vinery, Hougue du Pommier, on 19 and 20 September before finishing at Edible Guernsey in St Saviour's on 26 and 27 September.

Artist Emma Griffin said the idea grew out of an earlier exhibition with fellow artist James Kail at Guernsey Museum.

She explained: "We thought, why don't we take it out of the gallery and into a greenhouse and turn a greenhouse into an art gallery?"

Unlike many exhibitions, the artworks are being displayed inside working greenhouses, allowing visitors to meet growers and learn more about the island's agricultural industry.

Griffin said artists wanted to celebrate an industry that had played a major role in Guernsey's history but had declined in recent decades as many greenhouses disappeared or were replaced by housing.

For Griffin, the project is also personal. Her great-uncle, Michael Bourgaize, founded a well-known strawberry farm on the island, while other members of her family worked in the growing industry.

She said: "My granddad and my mum's first job was actually working in a greenhouse."

The exhibition has already attracted strong interest, with visitors sharing memories of family greenhouses on an interactive map.

Griffin said organisers hoped the project would inspire more islanders to grow their own food and reflect on Guernsey's agricultural roots.

articles.title: Bergerac director finds Jersey a real revelation
articles.summary: Director Paul  Wilmhurst and crew member Finn Lumsden reflect on filming the TV series in Jersey.
articles.body:
As the filming of the third series of Bergerac is under way, the director and a local crew member consider the important part Jersey plays in the TV show.

The first time director Paul Wilmhurst visited Jersey was to look for filming locations and he said it had been "a real revelation".

He said: "It feels very friendly, relaxed, it's like England but not England, as there's this slight sort of French continental vibe, but it's not too heavy, and I'm loving that and loving being here.

"There's something ironic really because I was reading about the crime statistics here and there aren't a lot of murders in Jersey, they don't really happen.

"I guess there's something about Bergerac that makes it kind of appealing in a way that you take somewhere very peaceful, and there's a sense of community, and a sense of people knowing each other, and then you tell these quite dark stories.

"It makes it a bit more sinister in a way."

Islander Finn Lumsden worked as a trainee on the second series and was invited back for the third.

He said: "I think we've managed to prove that it is possible, even if you're from Jersey, to get into this industry and really excel.

"It's quite amazing, I think I'm more starstruck now to when I started, it just feels great being able to leave the house and come and do this at home, which I never really thought I'd be able to do.

"It's a great privilege to be filming and especially Bergerac and it's just such a good heritage for the island."

Visit Jersey analysed the benefits it considered the new Bergerac series had brought to the island since it started filming in 2024.

The tourism group said one in four visitors to Jersey in 2025 had watched that first series and a YouGov survey found people who had watched both series were three times more likely to consider visiting Jersey in the next two years.

Visit Jersey said the production team spent £1.5m in the island's tourism and hospitality businesses, including 1,990 hotel room nights, during the filming of the first two series.

During those productions a total of 16 trainees from Jersey were employed, 380 islanders appeared on screen, 35 local crew members were employed and six actors from Jersey were cast in roles, the organisation added.

Wilmshurst said the new episodes involved an unsolved murder case in which a body was found in a cave on a beach with ritualistic elements 20 years ago.

He said: "It's one of those things where it's like, it could be one of this group of friends, it could be someone who taught them, there's a politician who's involved and maybe there's something going on in the police.

"So there's a lot of kind of feeling of who can I trust, where do I turn, what's really happening, and what is a fantasy and what is a real memory and what is evidence."

On Tuesday night St Helier Honorary Police closed the tunnel for an hour while some filming for the new season took place.

They said the filming took place inside the tunnel around dusk, which had enabled the production team to make the most of the lighting conditions needed for the scenes being captured.

A spokesperson joked officers could not reveal what was being filmed and curious people would have to watch the new season to find out.
